```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Facts about the designs, straight from the settings.
sa <- SETTINGS$analysts
n_geno <- length(sa$rep_counts)
n_analysts <- sum(sa$rep_counts)
n_two_plot <- sum(sa$rep_counts == 2)
n_one_plot <- sum(sa$rep_counts == 1)
n_family <- n_geno / sa$family_size
n_block <- ceiling(n_analysts / sa$block_size)
n_rep <- res$summary$n_rep
k_top <- round(SETTINGS$top_frac * n_geno)

# The hook: the first replicate (by seed) of the spurious-family experiment in
# which Analyst A's likelihood-ratio test is "significant" at 5%.
sp <- res$spurious
hook <- sp[which(sp$lrt > LRT_CRIT)[1], ]
hook_p <- 0.5 * pchisq(hook$lrt, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
# The prose says the two analysts advance different top-10% lists.
stopifnot(hook$topk_A != hook$topk_B)
```

### Introduction: The Higher-Likelihood Trap

Two analysts receive the same field trial: `r n_geno` genotypes, `r n_two_plot` of them planted in two plots and the other `r n_one_plot` in a single plot (`r n_analysts` plots in total, a partially replicated design). The genotypes come from `r n_family` families of `r sa$family_size` genotypes each. Both analysts fit a linear mixed model with a random genotype effect, estimate the variance components by REML, and rank the genotypes by their predicted genetic values (BLUPs). The top `r k_top` genotypes (the top 10%) will be advanced.

- **Analyst B** fits genotype only.
- **Analyst A** adds a random family effect. Their REML log-likelihood goes up, from `r fmt(hook$loglik_B, 2)` to `r fmt(hook$loglik_A, 2)`, and the formal likelihood-ratio test agrees: statistic `r fmt(hook$lrt, 2)`, p = `r fmt(hook_p, 3)` against the standard boundary-corrected reference ($\tfrac12\chi^2_0 + \tfrac12\chi^2_1$, a large-sample approximation). The family variance is estimated at `r fmt(hook$sigma2_extra_hat, 3)`.

Analyst A predicts each genotype as its own effect plus its family's effect, so the two analysts advance different lists. Whose list would you trust? Most of us would pick Analyst A: the model "fits better", and the test says the family effect is real.

This article is about why that instinct can be wrong. A higher REML log-likelihood means that the variance parameters explain the *observed* data better under the assumed model. It does not guarantee more accurate predictions of the genetic values we select on. Accuracy depends on which terms the model contains and where their variance estimates land (an extra term whose variance is estimated above zero changes every prediction), not on the height of the likelihood. The numbers we report from a trial, such as heritability and predicted gain, also depend on how well the data pin those estimates down.

There is a second, related habit. Anyone who has fitted mixed models in ASReml has seen this message:

```
Warning: Log-likelihood not converged
```

The usual response is to run `update()` until the warning goes away, or to ignore it because the BLUPs barely change. We will come back to this warning later and see what it does and does not put at risk.

To answer these questions honestly we need to know the truth, so everything here is **simulated**: the true genetic value of every genotype is known, and accuracy is measured directly as the correlation between predicted and true genetic values, plus the share of the true top 10% that each analyst selects. All models are fitted with a short REML/BLUP "oracle" in base R with dense linear algebra, shown in full; no commercial or specialized mixed-model software produces any result. Each experiment is repeated over `r n_rep` simulated trials with fixed seeds, so we report how often a pattern holds, not one lucky example.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Myth 1 statistics, computed here because the summary box below uses them.
analysts_tbl <- function(d) {
  d <- d[is.na(d$error), ]
  higher <- d$loglik_A - d$loglik_B > LOGLIK_TOL
  both_ok <- !d$degenerate_A & !d$degenerate_B
  worse <- d$cor_A < d$cor_B
  signif <- d$lrt > LRT_CRIT
  list(
    n = nrow(d),
    n_extra_pos = sum(d$sigma2_extra_hat > 0),
    n_higher_raw = sum(d$loglik_A > d$loglik_B),
    n_higher = sum(higher),
    p_higher = mean(higher),
    n_higher_ok = sum(higher & both_ok),
    p_worse_higher = mean(worse[higher & both_ok]),
    n_signif = sum(signif),
    n_signif_ok = sum(signif & both_ok),
    n_worse_signif = sum(worse[signif & both_ok]),
    p_signif = mean(signif),
    cor_A = mean(d$cor_A[both_ok]),
    cor_B = mean(d$cor_B[both_ok]),
    topk_A = mean(d$topk_A[both_ok]),
    topk_B = mean(d$topk_B[both_ok]),
    deg_A = sum(d$degenerate_A),
    deg_B = sum(d$degenerate_B)
  )
}
s_sp <- analysts_tbl(res$spurious)
s_rb <- analysts_tbl(res$real)
max_rounding <- with(res$spurious, max(abs(lrt[sigma2_extra_hat == 0])) / 2)
# Correlation between the LRT and A's accuracy gain, over the trials where A's
# log-likelihood is higher and both predictions are defined.
lrt_vs_gain <- function(d) {
  h <- is.na(d$error) & d$loglik_A - d$loglik_B > LOGLIK_TOL &
    !d$degenerate_A & !d$degenerate_B
  ct <- cor.test(d$lrt[h], d$cor_A[h] - d$cor_B[h])
  list(r = unname(ct$estimate), lo = ct$conf.int[1], hi = ct$conf.int[2],
       includes_zero = ct$conf.int[1] < 0 && ct$conf.int[2] > 0)
}
dc_sp <- lrt_vs_gain(res$spurious)
dc_rb <- lrt_vs_gain(res$real)
ci2 <- function(x) paste0(fmt(x$r, 2), " (95% CI ", fmt(x$lo, 2), " to ", fmt(x$hi, 2), ")")

# Direction words in the prose below; knitting stops if a rerun changes them.
stopifnot(
  s_sp$p_higher < 0.5,                 # "the share is usually lower" than half
  s_sp$p_worse_higher > 0.5,           # "usually less accurate"
  s_sp$cor_A < s_sp$cor_B,             # spurious: A's mean accuracy lower
  s_rb$cor_A > s_rb$cor_B,             # real block: A's mean accuracy higher
  s_rb$p_worse_higher < 0.5,           # real block: A less accurate "only" in a minority
  s_rb$p_worse_higher > 0,             # real block: "though not all of them"
  dc_sp$hi < 0 || dc_sp$includes_zero, # spurious: the two branches of the inline text
  dc_rb$includes_zero || abs(dc_rb$r) < 0.3   # real block: "a weak ... tendency"
)
# Rejection rate of the LRT under the null, with a binomial 95% CI.
sig_ci <- binom.test(s_sp$n_signif, s_sp$n)$conf.int

# Theory for a useless extra term (math packet, E3c): in a balanced one-way
# layout with b levels of the extra term, m units in each and no true effect,
# REML estimates its variance above zero, and so raises the log-likelihood,
# exactly when the between-level mean square exceeds the within-level one:
# P(F_{b-1, b(m-1)} > 1). We use m = our family size.
p_pos <- function(b, m = sa$family_size) 1 - pf(1, b - 1, b * (m - 1))
p_pos_2 <- p_pos(2)
p_pos_nf <- p_pos(n_family)
stopifnot(
  all(diff(p_pos(2:500)) > 0), p_pos(500) < 0.5,   # "rising towards 50%"
  p_pos(1e5) > 0.49                                # ... and approaching it
)
```

<div class="glance">

**The four myths at a glance**

1. **"A higher log-likelihood means better predictions."** Not necessarily. A random term that does not exist still raised the log-likelihood in `r pct(s_sp$p_higher)` of our simulated trials, and when it did, the predictions were usually less accurate (`r pct(s_sp$p_worse_higher)` of those trials). Across trials or datasets, log-likelihoods are not comparable at all.
2. **"The estimate is all that matters."** A variance estimate in the wrong place changes what you *report* (heritability, predicted gain, reliability) far more than which lines you *select*, as long as the genotypes are unrelated and similarly replicated. With a genomic relationship matrix, or with very uneven replication, the rankings move too.
3. **"All trials are equally trustworthy."** No. Weak trials give flat hills: scattered variance estimates and boundary fits with zero genetic variance. Intervals built from standard errors change with the scale they are built on, do not exist for boundary fits, and in weak trials usually reach below zero on the heritability scale. Profile-likelihood intervals have none of these problems and show honestly how little such a trial knows.
4. **"'Not converged' is just a warning."** It is a warning about every number that should come from the top of the hill (the log-likelihood, likelihood-ratio tests, variance components, heritability), even when the rankings of a simple genotype model barely change.

**So how do you choose between models?** Cross-validation over held-out plots and the boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test detect whether an extra term is real; neither tells you which model will predict better on the trial in front of you. The [practical checklist](#practical-checklist) at the end turns all of this into a short list of rules.

</div>

### The likelihood hill

Most of what follows can be read off one picture. For a model with a genotype effect and a residual, the REML log-likelihood depends on the variance components only through their ratio, which we can express as a heritability, $h^2 = \sigma^2_g / (\sigma^2_g + \sigma^2_e)$, once the residual variance is set to its best value for each $h^2$. Plotting that *profile* log-likelihood against $h^2$ gives a hill. Here $h^2$ is broad-sense heritability on a plot basis (what many breeders write as $H^2$); programs usually report heritability on an entry-mean basis, which is higher whenever entries have several plots (Cullis, Smith and Coombes 2006; Piepho and Möhring 2007).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cv <- res$curves
gamma_hat <- attr(cv, "gamma_hat")
gamma_true <- attr(cv, "gamma_true")
h2_hat <- gamma_hat / (1 + gamma_hat)
h2_true <- gamma_true / (1 + gamma_true)
ll_max <- max(cv$loglik)

# Values of h2 within qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2 log-likelihood units of the peak:
# an approximate 95% profile-likelihood interval.
drop_95 <- qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2
top <- cv$h2[cv$loglik >= ll_max - drop_95]
h2_lo <- min(top)
h2_hi <- max(top)

sb <- SETTINGS$baseline
n_base <- sum(sb$rep_counts)
n_base_two <- sum(sb$rep_counts == 2)
n_base_one <- sum(sb$rep_counts == 1)
```

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
hill <- subset(cv, loglik >= ll_max - 12)
ggplot(hill, aes(h2, loglik)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = h2_lo, xmax = h2_hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = col_main, alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(colour = col_main, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = h2_hat, colour = col_accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = h2_true, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = h2_hat, y = ll_max - 10.5, label = "REML estimate (peak)",
           colour = col_accent, size = 3.6, hjust = -0.05, label.size = 0) +
  annotate("label", x = h2_true, y = ll_max - 10.5, label = "true h²",
           colour = col_ink, size = 3.6, hjust = 1.05, label.size = 0) +
  labs(title = "The likelihood hill for one simulated trial",
       x = expression("Heritability " * h^2 * " (plot level)"),
       y = "Profile REML log-likelihood") +
  my_theme
```

This is one simulated trial of the baseline design (`r n_base_two` genotypes with two plots, `r n_base_one` with one; true $h^2$ = `r fmt(h2_true, 1)`). Three features of the hill matter, and only two of them are about the variance estimate:

- **Where the peak sits.** The REML estimate is the top of the hill, here $\hat h^2$ = `r fmt(h2_hat, 3)`. It is not the true value (`r fmt(h2_true, 1)`): it is the value that best explains *this* dataset, noise included.
- **How wide the hill is.** The shaded band holds the values of $h^2$ whose log-likelihood is within `r fmt(drop_95, 2)` units of the peak, roughly a 95% profile-likelihood interval: from `r fmt(h2_lo, 2)` to `r fmt(h2_hi, 2)`. A flat, wide hill means the data cannot tell those values apart.
- **How high the peak is.** The peak value, `r fmt(ll_max, 1)`, is a property of this dataset. On its own it says nothing about how good the predictions are.

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** the REML log-likelihood tells you which variance components best explain the data you have. Its peak is your estimate and its width is your uncertainty. Its height is not a score for prediction quality, and in the rest of the article we will keep asking what the height can and cannot tell us.

</div>

### Building the oracle

We use the standard model for a single trial:

$$y = X\beta + Zg + e, \qquad g \sim N(0, \sigma^2_g I), \qquad e \sim N(0, \sigma^2_e I),$$

where $y$ holds the plot values, $X\beta$ is the fixed part (here just an overall mean), $Z$ assigns plots to genotypes, $g$ are the genetic values we want to predict, and $e$ is the plot error. In the simulations $\sigma^2_g + \sigma^2_e = 1$, so $\sigma^2_g$ is the plot-level (broad-sense) heritability.

REML ("restricted" or "residual" maximum likelihood; Patterson and Thompson 1971; Harville 1977) estimates $\sigma^2_g$ and $\sigma^2_e$ from the part of the data that is free of the fixed effects: think of it as first removing the overall mean, then asking which variance components make the remaining contrasts between plots most probable. The BLUPs then come from Henderson's mixed model equations (Henderson 1975). Computed with estimated variance components instead of the true ones, as they always are in practice, they are strictly *empirical* BLUPs; we call them BLUPs for short.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Under the hood: how REML works (the formulas)</summary>

For variance components $\theta = (\sigma^2_g, \sigma^2_e)$, with $V = \sigma^2_g ZZ' + \sigma^2_e I$ and $p$ fixed-effect parameters among $n$ plots, the REML log-likelihood is

<div style="font-size: 85%">
$$\ell_R(\theta) = -\tfrac12\left[(n-p)\log 2\pi + \log|V| + \log|X'V^{-1}X| + y'Py\right], \quad P = V^{-1} - V^{-1}X(X'V^{-1}X)^{-1}X'V^{-1}.$$
</div>

Written as the likelihood of $n-p$ orthonormal error contrasts $K'y$ (with $K'X = 0$), it differs from $\ell_R$ only by the constant $\tfrac12\log|X'X|$, which does not depend on $\theta$. Different programs report different constants, which is one more reason not to compare log-likelihood values across programs.

With $\gamma = \sigma^2_g/\sigma^2_e$, one eigendecomposition $K'ZZ'K = UDU'$ and $w = U'K'y$ give the whole hill cheaply. The residual variance has a closed form for each $\gamma$, and the profile log-likelihood is

<div style="font-size: 85%">
$$\hat\sigma^2_e(\gamma) = \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_j \frac{w_j^2}{1+\gamma d_j}, \qquad \ell(\gamma) = -\tfrac12\left[(n-p)(\log 2\pi + 1) + (n-p)\log\hat\sigma^2_e(\gamma) + \sum_j \log(1+\gamma d_j)\right].$$
</div>

The BLUPs solve the mixed model equations with $\lambda = 1/\gamma$:

<div style="font-size: 85%">
$$\begin{bmatrix} X'X & X'Z \\ Z'X & Z'Z + \lambda I \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \hat\beta \\ \hat g \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X'y \\ Z'y \end{bmatrix}.$$
</div>

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** after removing the mean, the data are rotated so that each piece is independent; the log-likelihood then becomes a simple sum that is cheap to evaluate for any heritability. The REML estimate is the heritability where that sum is highest. The BLUP of a genotype shrinks its observed deviation from the mean towards zero, and genotypes with fewer plots are shrunk more.

</div>

The whole oracle fits on one screen, and we checked it against a naive computation before trusting it.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Under the hood: the oracle code and how we checked it</summary>

`reml_fit()` searches a fine grid of `r length(SETTINGS$log_gamma_grid)` values of $\log\gamma$ (plus $\gamma = 0$, the boundary where $\hat\sigma^2_g = 0$), then refines the best grid point with `optimize()`, so we can be confident we have the global maximum of the hill and not just a local bump:

```{r, file="R/oracle.R", eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Small check, run when knitting: rebuild the trial of the hill figure
# (baseline design, replicate 1) and compare the fast eigen path with the
# naive dense computation from the full n x n matrix V.
seed_1 <- BASE_SEED + 1
design_1 <- make_design(sb$rep_counts, seed = seed_1)
sim_1 <- simulate_trial(design_1, h2 = sb$h2, seed = seed_1)
dm_1 <- design_matrices(design_1)
setup_1 <- reml_setup(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z)
fit_1 <- reml_fit(setup_1)

check_gammas <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 2, 20)
fast <- reml_loglik(check_gammas, setup_1)
naive <- vapply(check_gammas, function(g) {
  se <- reml_sigma2_e(g, setup_1)
  reml_loglik_naive(g * se, se, sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z)
}, numeric(1))
max_diff_naive <- max(abs(fast - naive))
grid_gap <- fit_1$loglik - max(fit_1$grid$loglik)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fit_1$gamma, gamma_hat, tolerance = 1e-8)), grid_gap >= 0)
```

On the trial of the hill figure, the fast eigen-based log-likelihood and a naive computation that builds and factorizes the full `r n_base` &times; `r n_base` variance matrix agree to within `r sci(max_diff_naive)` at `r length(check_gammas)` values of $\gamma$ between `r min(check_gammas)` and `r max(check_gammas)`. The refined maximum is `r sci(grid_gap)` log-likelihood units above the best grid point (the code keeps the grid point if the optimizer ever does worse), and it is the same estimate stored in the results, $\hat\gamma$ = `r fmt(fit_1$gamma, 3)`. The test suite in the repository runs the same comparisons on more designs, including a balanced design where REML has a closed-form answer.

</details>

### Myth 1: A higher log-likelihood means better predictions

#### Two analysts, two worlds

The trial in the introduction was simulated, so we can ask how it ends. We repeated the two-analyst comparison over `r n_rep` independent trials of the same design, in two different worlds:

- **Spurious family.** There is no family effect at all: genotypes in the same family are no more alike than any others. Analyst A's family term is pure noise. (The trial in the introduction came from this world.) Read "family" as any grouping label with no real variance behind it (a wrong pedigree assignment, seed lot, tray).
- **Real block.** The field has a real block effect: consecutive groups of `r sa$block_size` plots (`r n_block` incomplete blocks) share a random block effect with variance `r fmt(sa$sigma2_block, 2)` (the genetic variance is `r fmt(sa$h2, 1)`). In this world Analyst A adds a block term instead of a family term, and that term is correct.

Analyst B always fits genotype only. Because A's model contains B's as the special case where the extra variance is zero, A's maximized log-likelihood can never be lower than B's.

In the **spurious-family** world, Analyst A's log-likelihood was higher in `r pct(s_sp$p_higher)` of the trials, even though the family effect does not exist, and in `r pct(s_sp$p_worse_higher)` of those trials A's predictions were *less* accurate than B's. The likelihood-ratio test called the family effect "significant" in `r s_sp$n_signif` of `r s_sp$n` trials, and A was less accurate than B in `r if (s_sp$n_worse_signif == s_sp$n_signif_ok) paste('every one of those', s_sp$n_signif_ok, 'trials') else paste(s_sp$n_worse_signif, 'of those', s_sp$n_signif_ok, 'trials')`. A's mean accuracy was also lower (`r fmt(s_sp$cor_A)` vs `r fmt(s_sp$cor_B)`).

In the **real-block** world, A's log-likelihood was higher in `r pct(s_rb$p_higher)` of the trials, and A was less accurate in only `r pct(s_rb$p_worse_higher)` of those. Modeling the blocks removes field noise from the genotype comparisons, and A's mean accuracy is higher (`r fmt(s_rb$cor_A)` vs `r fmt(s_rb$cor_B)`).

So the same observation, "A's log-likelihood is higher", goes with worse predictions in one world and better predictions in the other. The log-likelihood comparison cannot tell you which world you are in.

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
both <- bind_rows(
  res$spurious |> mutate(world = "Spurious family (A is wrong)"),
  res$real |> mutate(world = "Real block (A is right)")
) |>
  filter(is.na(error), !degenerate_A, !degenerate_B) |>
  mutate(world = factor(world, levels = c("Spurious family (A is wrong)",
                                          "Real block (A is right)")),
         d_cor = cor_A - cor_B,
         lrt = pmax(lrt, 0))

ggplot(both, aes(lrt, d_cor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = LRT_CRIT, colour = col_accent, linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = col_main, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ world, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Gain in log-likelihood vs gain in accuracy (A minus B)",
       x = "Likelihood-ratio statistic, 2 × (logL A − logL B)",
       y = "Accuracy of A − accuracy of B") +
  my_theme
```

Each point is one simulated trial; the dashed line is the 5% LRT cutoff and points above zero are trials where Analyst A predicted better.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Why not "half the time"? What theory says</summary>

You may have read that a useless extra variance component raises the log-likelihood "half the time". That rule comes from large-sample theory and needs many levels of the extra effect; with a modest number of levels the share is usually lower. In a balanced design where each level of the extra term holds `r sa$family_size` units (like our families of `r sa$family_size` genotypes, with one plot each) and the term does not exist, the log-likelihood rises exactly when the extra variance is estimated above zero, and theory puts that chance at about `r pct(p_pos_2)` for an extra term with 2 levels, rising towards 50% as the number of levels grows (`r pct(p_pos_nf)` for `r n_family` levels). With `r n_family` families we saw `r pct(s_sp$p_higher)`.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (full table, test details and counts)</summary>

When A's extra variance is estimated as exactly zero, the two models are the same model and the two log-likelihoods differ only by rounding (at most `r sci(max_rounding)` here). A naive "is A larger?" comparison would call A higher in `r s_sp$n_higher_raw` of `r s_sp$n` spurious-family trials, `r s_sp$n_higher_raw - s_sp$n_higher` of them only because of that rounding noise. We count A as higher only when its log-likelihood exceeds B's by more than `r sci(LOGLIK_TOL)`.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
row_names <- c(
  "Trials",
  "Extra variance estimated above zero",
  "A's log-likelihood higher",
  "A less accurate than B, when A's log-likelihood is higher",
  "LRT \"significant\" at 5%",
  "A less accurate than B, when the LRT is significant",
  "Mean accuracy, cor(predicted, true): A",
  "Mean accuracy, cor(predicted, true): B",
  "Mean share of true top 10% selected: A",
  "Mean share of true top 10% selected: B",
  "Degenerate predictions (genetic variance = 0): A / B"
)
col_for <- function(s) c(
  s$n,
  s$n_extra_pos,
  paste0(s$n_higher, " (", pct(s$p_higher), ")"),
  paste0(pct(s$p_worse_higher), " (of ", s$n_higher_ok, ")"),
  paste0(s$n_signif, " (", pct(s$p_signif), ")"),
  paste0(s$n_worse_signif, " of ", s$n_signif_ok),
  fmt(s$cor_A), fmt(s$cor_B),
  fmt(s$topk_A), fmt(s$topk_B),
  paste0(s$deg_A, " / ", s$deg_B)
)
data.frame(
  Quantity = row_names,
  `Spurious family (A is wrong)` = col_for(s_sp),
  `Real block (A is right)` = col_for(s_rb),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

Accuracy comparisons in the table use only the trials where both analysts' predictions are defined. When REML estimates the genetic variance as zero, every genotype gets the same prediction (zero), so a correlation or a top-10% list does not exist. Those trials are counted in the last row, not hidden. The LRT uses the 5% cutoff of the standard boundary-corrected reference, an even mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$ (cutoff `r fmt(LRT_CRIT, 2)`). That reference is a large-sample approximation (Self and Liang 1987; Stram and Lee 1994 for mixed models), and it needs many levels of the extra effect to be accurate (Crainiceanu and Ruppert 2004).

In the spurious-family world the test's rejection rate was `r pct(s_sp$p_signif)` at a nominal 5% (95% CI `r pct(sig_ci[1])` to `r pct(sig_ci[2])`)`r if (sig_ci[1] <= 0.05 && sig_ci[2] >= 0.05) paste0(', within simulation noise of the nominal rate with ', n_family, ' families') else if (sig_ci[2] < 0.05) paste0(': with only ', n_family, ' families the large-sample reference is conservative here') else paste0(': with only ', n_family, ' families the large-sample reference is liberal here')`. The trial in the introduction was the first of the "significant" trials.

Among the trials where A's log-likelihood was higher, the correlation between the LRT statistic and A's accuracy gain was `r ci2(dc_sp)` in the spurious-family world: `r if (dc_sp$hi < 0) 'trials where A gained more log-likelihood from the family term tended to be the ones where its predictions lost more' else 'the interval includes zero, so there is no clear pattern'`. In the real-block world it was `r ci2(dc_rb)`, `r if (dc_rb$includes_zero) 'an interval that includes zero' else if (dc_rb$lo > 0) 'a weak positive tendency' else 'a weak negative tendency'`, and `r pct(1 - s_rb$p_worse_higher)` of those trials sit above zero, though not all of them.

</details>

#### Replicate trials of one design

```{r, echo=FALSE}
designs <- c(weak = "Weak", baseline = "Baseline", strong = "Strong")
rep_stats <- lapply(names(designs), function(sc) {
  d <- res[[sc]]
  d <- d[is.na(d$error), ]
  ok <- !d$degenerate
  ct <- cor.test(d$loglik_max[ok], d$cor[ok])
  s <- SETTINGS[[sc]]
  list(n = nrow(d), n_boundary = sum(d$boundary), n_cor = sum(ok),
       r = unname(ct$estimate), lo = ct$conf.int[1], hi = ct$conf.int[2],
       includes_zero = ct$conf.int[1] < 0 && ct$conf.int[2] > 0,
       h2 = s$h2, n_plots = sum(s$rep_counts),
       mean_cor = mean(d$cor[ok]))
})
names(rep_stats) <- names(designs)
rw <- rep_stats$weak; rbase <- rep_stats$baseline; rst <- rep_stats$strong
# "If anything, the relationship goes the other way" and the takeaway's
# "negative in the baseline and strong designs" rely on these.
stopifnot(rep_stats$baseline$hi < 0, rep_stats$strong$hi < 0)
ci_txt <- function(s) paste0(fmt(s$r, 2), " (95% CI ", fmt(s$lo, 2), " to ", fmt(s$hi, 2), ")")

ss <- SETTINGS$strong
n_strong_three <- sum(ss$rep_counts == 3)
n_strong_two <- sum(ss$rep_counts == 2)
```

The two analysts compared two models on the same data. A different temptation is to compare different trials of the same design: this season's trial reached a higher log-likelihood than last season's, so is it more reliable? We simulated `r n_rep` trials of each of three designs and fitted the genotype model to each:

- **Weak:** the baseline layout (`r n_base_two` genotypes with two plots, `r n_base_one` with one; `r rw$n_plots` plots) with $h^2$ = `r fmt(rw$h2, 1)`.
- **Baseline:** the same layout with $h^2$ = `r fmt(rbase$h2, 1)`.
- **Strong:** `r n_strong_three` genotypes with three plots and `r n_strong_two` with two (`r rst$n_plots` plots), $h^2$ = `r fmt(rst$h2, 1)`.

Trials where REML put the genetic variance at zero (the boundary of the hill) have no defined accuracy, because all predictions are equal, so they are left out here; Myth 3 returns to them.

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=11, fig.height=4.2, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
rep_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(designs), function(sc) {
  res[[sc]] |>
    filter(is.na(error), !degenerate) |>
    mutate(design = paste0(designs[[sc]], ": cor = ", fmt(rep_stats[[sc]]$r, 2)))
})) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = unique(design)))

ggplot(rep_df, aes(loglik_max, cor)) +
  geom_point(colour = col_main, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = col_accent,
              linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ design, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Maximum log-likelihood vs accuracy across replicate trials",
       x = "Maximized REML log-likelihood",
       y = "Accuracy, cor(predicted, true)") +
  my_theme
```

Within a design, the trials with a *higher* maximum log-likelihood did not have more accurate predictions. If anything, the relationship goes the other way: the correlation between the two was `r fmt(rbase$r, 2)` in the baseline design and `r fmt(rst$r, 2)` in the strong design. In the weak design it was `r fmt(rw$r, 2)`, and its 95% interval `r if (rw$includes_zero) "includes zero, so that design alone does not tell us the sign" else "excludes zero"`.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (intervals and counts)</summary>

The correlations between the maximized log-likelihood and accuracy, with 95% confidence intervals, were `r ci_txt(rbase)` in the baseline design, `r ci_txt(rst)` in the strong design and `r ci_txt(rw)` in the weak design; the weak interval `r if (rw$includes_zero) "includes zero: the relationship there is weak at best" else "excludes zero"`.

In `r rw$n_boundary` of the `r rw$n` weak trials (`r pct(rw$n_boundary / rw$n)`), REML put the genetic variance at zero, the boundary of the hill. That also happened in `r rbase$n_boundary` baseline trials and `r rst$n_boundary` strong trials. These trials have no defined accuracy (all predictions are equal), so the figure and the correlations above use the remaining `r rw$n_cor`, `r rbase$n_cor` and `r rst$n_cor` trials.

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** the log-likelihood of a trial mostly measures how much the plot values vary, and more spread means a lower log-likelihood. A trial whose genotypes happen to differ more than usual has more spread in its data, so its log-likelihood is lower. But larger genetic differences are also easier to detect, so its predictions are more accurate. The same trial gets a lower log-likelihood and better predictions.

</div>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Under the hood: why the correlation is negative</summary>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Approximate correlation for a balanced trial with r plots per genotype:
# -sqrt(H2_r / (2 r)), where H2_r = r / (r + lambda) and lambda = (1 - h2) / h2.
balanced_cor <- function(h2, r) {
  lambda <- (1 - h2) / h2
  -sqrt((r / (r + lambda)) / (2 * r))
}
ex_r <- 2
ex_h2 <- 0.3
ex_cor <- balanced_cor(ex_h2, ex_r)
```

In a balanced trial with $m$ genotypes and $r$ plots each, the maximized REML log-likelihood is, up to a constant,
$$\ell_{\max} = -\tfrac12\left[(m-1)\log \text{MSB} + m(r-1)\log \text{MSW}\right],$$
where MSB and MSW are the between- and within-genotype mean squares of the ANOVA (when the genetic variance estimate is positive). A larger realized genetic spread raises MSB and lowers $\ell_{\max}$, while it raises the accuracy. For a balanced trial, this gives an approximate correlation of $-\sqrt{H^2_r/(2r)}$ across replicate trials, where $H^2_r = r/(r + \lambda)$ is the entry-mean heritability and $\lambda = \sigma^2_e/\sigma^2_g$. For example, $r$ = `r ex_r` and $h^2$ = `r fmt(ex_h2, 1)` give `r fmt(ex_cor, 2)`. Our designs are unbalanced, so this formula is only a guide; the simulation above is the evidence.

</details>

#### Across trials and designs: not comparable

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Changing units multiplies y by a constant c and shifts the REML
# log-likelihood by -(n - p) log(c), whatever the data.
unit_c <- 1000
fit_kg <- reml_fit(reml_setup(sim_1$y * unit_c, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z))
unit_shift <- fit_kg$loglik - fit_1$loglik
unit_shift_theory <- -(setup_1$n - setup_1$p) * log(unit_c)
# Same heritability estimate and the same ranking of genotypes after the change.
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(fit_kg$gamma, fit_1$gamma, tolerance = 1e-6)),
  identical(rank(blup(sim_1$y * unit_c, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z, fit_kg$gamma)$g),
            rank(blup(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z, fit_1$gamma)$g))
)
rng <- function(sc) range(res[[sc]]$loglik_max, na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(unit_shift, unit_shift_theory)),
  unit_shift < 0,                          # kg lowers it, so tonnes "raises it"
  rst$mean_cor - rbase$mean_cor > 0.1      # strong trials "predict far better"
)
```

Log-likelihoods of different trials are not even on the same scale. The strong trials predict far better than the baseline ones (mean accuracy `r fmt(rst$mean_cor, 2)` against `r fmt(rbase$mean_cor, 2)`), but the gap between their log-likelihoods says nothing about that (the figure above uses free axes on purpose). The level of a log-likelihood depends on things that have nothing to do with prediction quality:

- **The amount of data.** Every residual degree of freedom adds a term to the log-likelihood, so trials with different numbers of plots sit on different scales.
- **The units.** Recording the yield of the hill trial in kilograms instead of tonnes moves its maximized log-likelihood by `r fmt(unit_shift, 1)`, with the same heritability estimate and the same ranking of genotypes; going back to tonnes raises it by the same amount. Whether a comparison across datasets goes up or down can depend on nothing more than the units.
- **Transformations.** A log or square-root transformation of the trait changes the data being modeled, so the log-likelihoods of the two analyses are on different scales.
- **The fixed effects.** REML is the likelihood of the data *after* the fixed effects have been removed, so models with different fixed effects describe different sets of contrasts and their REML log-likelihoods are not comparable, even on the same data. To compare fixed effects, use maximum likelihood or the adjusted REML comparison of Welham and Thompson (1997).

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (log-likelihood ranges and the units check)</summary>

The log-likelihoods of the baseline trials range from `r fmt(rng("baseline")[1], 0)` to `r fmt(rng("baseline")[2], 0)`, while those of the strong trials range from `r fmt(rng("strong")[1], 0)` to `r fmt(rng("strong")[2], 0)`. Multiplying every observation by a constant $c$ shifts the REML log-likelihood by $-(n-p)\log c$; for the change from tonnes to kilograms ($c$ = `r unit_c`) theory gives `r fmt(unit_shift_theory, 1)`, and the refit of the hill trial moved by `r fmt(unit_shift, 1)`.

</details>

Log-likelihoods are comparable only between models fitted to the same data, in the same units, with the same fixed effects, by the same program. Even then, as the two analysts showed, a bare comparison of the two numbers is not enough: judging whether the extra term is supported needs a proper test or cross-validation.

<div class="takeaway">

**Takeaway for breeders**

- Adding a random term that is not really there still raises the REML log-likelihood in a large share of trials (`r pct(s_sp$p_higher)` in our spurious-family simulation; in theory about `r pct(p_pos_2)` for a balanced extra term with 2 levels of `r sa$family_size` units each, rising towards 50% as the number of levels grows). When it did, the predictions were usually *less* accurate (`r pct(s_sp$p_worse_higher)` of those trials).
- The same "higher log-likelihood" came with better predictions when the extra term was real. The log-likelihood comparison alone cannot tell the two situations apart.
- Across replicate trials of one design, a higher log-likelihood did not mean better predictions; in the baseline and strong designs the relationship was negative.
- Never compare log-likelihoods across datasets, units, transformations, fixed effects or programs.

</div>

### Myth 2: The estimate is all that matters

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Value of a curve column at any gamma (linear interpolation on log gamma).
at_g <- function(d, col, g) approx(d$log_gamma, d[[col]], xout = log(g))$y
h2_of <- function(g) g / (1 + g)

ei <- res$exp_iid
g0 <- attr(ei, "gamma_true")
wrong <- 10                                   # "ten times too small / too large"
g_lo <- g0 / wrong
g_hi <- g0 * wrong

# Expected (average over replicate trials) values at the truth and 10x off.
e_at <- function(d, col) c(lo = at_g(d, col, g_lo), true = at_g(d, col, g0),
                           hi = at_g(d, col, g_hi))
ei_cor <- e_at(ei, "cor"); ei_topk <- e_at(ei, "topk")
ei_mse <- e_at(ei, "mse"); ei_gain <- e_at(ei, "gain_slope")
iid_cor_loss <- max(ei_cor["true"] - ei_cor[c("lo", "hi")])
sd_cor_base <- sd(res$baseline$cor, na.rm = TRUE)

# The single trial of the hill (baseline replicate 1).
s_cor <- c(lo = at_g(cv, "cor", g_lo), true = at_g(cv, "cor", g0),
           hat = at_g(cv, "cor", gamma_hat), hi = at_g(cv, "cor", g_hi))
s_topk <- c(lo = at_g(cv, "topk", g_lo), hat = at_g(cv, "topk", gamma_hat),
            hi = at_g(cv, "topk", g_hi))
range_h2 <- c(0.02, 0.9)
cv_win <- subset(cv, h2 >= range_h2[1] & h2 <= range_h2[2])
s_topk_range <- range(cv_win$topk) * k_top

# Expected accuracy is highest close to the true value; MSE lowest there.
h2_best_cor <- ei$h2[which.max(ei$cor)]
h2_best_mse <- ei$h2[which.min(ei$mse)]

# Direction words below; knitting stops if a rerun changes them.
stopifnot(
  iid_cor_loss > 0,
  iid_cor_loss < sd_cor_base / 2,         # "small next to" the trial-to-trial spread
  ei_gain["lo"] > 1, ei_gain["hi"] < 1,   # too small: under-promises; too large: over-promises
  ei_mse["true"] < min(ei_mse[c("lo", "hi")]),
  abs(h2_best_cor - h2_true) < 0.05, abs(h2_best_mse - h2_true) < 0.05,   # "both close to the true"
  abs(s_cor["hat"] - s_cor["true"]) < 0.02   # single trial: "slightly" better or worse
)
```

Suppose the REML estimate lands in the wrong place. How much does that cost? On the trial of the hill figure we computed the BLUPs at every point of the grid, not just at the peak, and scored each set of predictions against the true genetic values. We then averaged the same curves over all `r n_rep` baseline trials, to see what happens *in expectation* and not just on one dataset.

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=12, fig.height=7, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
ei_win <- subset(ei, h2 >= range_h2[1] & h2 <= range_h2[2])
lines_df <- bind_rows(
  cv_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "cor", value = cor, source = "This trial"),
  cv_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "topk", value = topk, source = "This trial"),
  cv_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "mse", value = mse, source = "This trial"),
  cv_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "gain", value = gain_slope, source = "This trial"),
  ei_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "cor", value = cor, source = "Average of 500 trials"),
  ei_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "topk", value = topk, source = "Average of 500 trials"),
  ei_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "mse", value = mse, source = "Average of 500 trials"),
  ei_win |> transmute(h2, metric = "gain", value = gain_slope, source = "Average of 500 trials")
) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = c("This trial", "Average of 500 trials")))
stopifnot(attr(ei, "n_rep") == 500)   # the legend label above

marks <- list(
  geom_vline(xintercept = h2_true, colour = col_ink, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6),
  geom_vline(xintercept = h2_hat, colour = col_accent, linewidth = 0.6)
)
panel <- function(m, title, ylab, ref = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(filter(lines_df, metric == m), aes(h2, value, colour = source)) +
    marks +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_main, col_third), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title, x = expression(h^2 * " used for the BLUPs"), y = ylab) +
    my_theme + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
  if (!is.null(ref)) p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = ref, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.4)
  p
}
p_ll <- ggplot(cv_win, aes(h2, loglik - ll_max)) +
  marks +
  geom_line(colour = col_main, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Log-likelihood (this trial)", x = expression(h^2 * " used for the BLUPs"),
       y = "Below the peak") +
  my_theme + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
p_cor <- panel("cor", "Accuracy, cor(predicted, true)", "Correlation")
p_topk <- panel("topk", "Share of the true top 10% selected", "Share")
p_mse <- panel("mse", "Mean squared error of the BLUPs", "MSE")
p_gain <- panel("gain", "Gain slope (1 = predicted gain is right)", "Slope (log scale)", ref = 1) +
  scale_y_log10()

p_ll + p_cor + p_topk + p_mse + p_gain + guide_area() +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3, guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(title = "What changes when the variance estimate lands elsewhere",
                  subtitle = "Dashed line: true h². Orange line: the REML estimate for this trial.",
                  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
                                plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))) &
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The x-axis is the heritability plugged into the mixed model equations, from `r fmt(range_h2[1], 2)` to `r fmt(range_h2[2], 1)`. Read the panels as "what if REML had landed here?".

- **Rankings hardly move.** Averaged over trials, the accuracy at the true value is `r fmt(ei_cor["true"])`; a variance ratio `r wrong` times too small gives `r fmt(ei_cor["lo"])`, and `r wrong` times too large gives `r fmt(ei_cor["hi"])`. That loss of at most `r fmt(iid_cor_loss, 3)` is small next to the ordinary trial-to-trial spread of accuracy in this design (standard deviation `r fmt(sd_cor_base, 3)`).
- **Scale moves a lot.** Over the same range the reported heritability runs from `r fmt(h2_of(g_lo), 2)` to `r fmt(h2_of(g_hi), 2)`, and the gain slope (the slope of the regression of true on predicted values, $g$ on $\hat g$, also called the dispersion or inflation slope) goes from `r fmt(ei_gain["true"], 2)` at the truth to `r fmt(ei_gain["lo"], 2)` and `r fmt(ei_gain["hi"], 2)`. A slope of `r fmt(ei_gain["hi"], 2)` means the selected lines deliver only about `r round(100 * ei_gain["hi"])`% of the gain the BLUPs promise; a slope above 1 means the BLUPs are shrunk too much and under-promise.
- **The truth wins on average, not on every trial.** Averaged over trials, accuracy and prediction error are best close to the true value. On the single trial of the hill, the REML estimate did `r if (s_cor["hat"] > s_cor["true"]) "slightly better than the truth, by luck" else "slightly worse than the truth"`. That is why every claim in this article is about behaviour across many trials.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (prediction error and the single trial)</summary>

The mean squared error of the BLUPs goes from `r fmt(ei_mse["true"])` at the truth to `r fmt(ei_mse["lo"])` and `r fmt(ei_mse["hi"])`. Averaged over trials, accuracy peaks at $h^2$ = `r fmt(h2_best_cor, 2)` and the error is lowest at `r fmt(h2_best_mse, 2)`, both close to the true `r fmt(h2_true, 1)`: BLUP with the true variance components is the best (minimum mean squared error) linear unbiased predictor in expectation (Henderson 1975). On the single trial, the BLUPs at the REML estimate had accuracy `r fmt(s_cor["hat"])` against `r fmt(s_cor["true"])` at the true value, `r if (s_cor["hat"] > s_cor["true"]) "slightly better: on one dataset the estimate can beat the truth by luck" else "slightly worse"`, and the number of true top-10% genotypes among the `r k_top` selected varied by at most `r diff(s_topk_range)` over the whole range shown.

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** in a simple genotype model, the variance estimate mostly decides *how much* the BLUPs are shrunk, not *in what order* the genotypes come out. When the genotypes have similar replication, which lines you select is robust to a poor estimate. What you report about them is not: heritability, the predicted genetic gain and the error of the predictions all depend directly on where the estimate landed.

</div>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Try it yourself: move the heritability with a slider</summary>

Drag the slider to move the heritability used for the BLUPs on the trial of the hill figure. The marker shows the log-likelihood (relative to the peak), the accuracy and the gain slope at that value.

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
w_idx <- which(cv$h2 >= range_h2[1] & cv$h2 <= range_h2[2])
w_idx <- w_idx[seq(1, length(w_idx), by = 2)]
wd <- cv[w_idx, ]
wd$ll_rel <- wd$loglik - ll_max
start_i <- which.min(abs(wd$h2 - h2_hat))

panel_ly <- function(y, name, ylab, ylog = FALSE) {
  p <- plotly::plot_ly(wd, x = ~h2)
  p <- plotly::add_lines(p, y = y, name = name, line = list(color = col_main, width = 2),
                         hoverinfo = "x+y")
  p <- plotly::add_markers(p, x = wd$h2[start_i], y = y[start_i], name = name,
                           marker = list(color = col_accent, size = 11), hoverinfo = "x+y")
  ax <- list(title = ylab, type = if (ylog) "log" else "linear")
  if (ylog) {
    ax$tickvals <- c(0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)
    ax$ticktext <- c("0.3", "0.5", "1", "2", "5", "10")
  }
  plotly::layout(p, yaxis = ax)
}
fig <- plotly::subplot(
  panel_ly(wd$ll_rel, "log-likelihood", "logL below peak"),
  panel_ly(wd$cor, "accuracy", "Accuracy"),
  panel_ly(wd$gain_slope, "gain slope", "Gain slope", ylog = TRUE),
  nrows = 3, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE
)
step_title <- function(i) {
  sprintf("h² = %.2f   |   logL %.1f below the peak   |   accuracy %.3f   |   gain slope %.2f",
          wd$h2[i], abs(wd$ll_rel[i]), wd$cor[i], wd$gain_slope[i])
}
steps <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(wd)), function(i) {
  list(method = "update",
       label = formatC(wd$h2[i], format = "f", digits = 2),
       args = list(list(x = list(list(wd$h2[i]), list(wd$h2[i]), list(wd$h2[i])),
                        y = list(list(wd$ll_rel[i]), list(wd$cor[i]), list(wd$gain_slope[i]))),
                   list(title = list(text = step_title(i), font = list(size = 13))),
                   list(1, 3, 5)))
})
plotly::layout(
  fig,
  showlegend = FALSE,
  title = list(text = step_title(start_i), font = list(size = 13)),
  xaxis = list(title = "h² used for the BLUPs"),
  margin = list(t = 60),
  sliders = list(list(active = start_i - 1, steps = steps,
                      currentvalue = list(prefix = "h² = ", font = list(color = col_ink)),
                      font = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"), minorticklen = 0,
                      pad = list(t = 50)))
) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Under the hood: why rankings barely move</summary>

When every genotype has the same number of plots $r$, the BLUP of genotype $i$ is $\hat{g}_i = \frac{r}{r+\lambda}(\bar{y}_i - \bar{y})$: every genotype's deviation from the trial mean is multiplied by the same factor. A different $\lambda$ changes that factor, but not the order of the genotypes, so in a balanced trial the correlation and the top-10% list do not depend on the variance estimate at all (as long as it is above zero). With partial replication the factor $r_i/(r_i+\lambda)$ differs between genotypes with one and two plots, and the GLS mean depends on $\lambda$ too, so rankings can move a little, which is why our designs are partially replicated. The loss is also *second order*: near the true value, the expected error of the BLUPs grows with the square of the distance from it, which is why the curves are so flat around the truth.

</details>

#### When genotypes are related: rankings move too

```{r, echo=FALSE}
kin_s <- SETTINGS$kinship
ek3 <- res$exp_kin[["h2_0.3"]]; ek1 <- res$exp_kin[["h2_0.1"]]
g0_k3 <- attr(ek3, "gamma_true"); g0_k1 <- attr(ek1, "gamma_true")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(h2_of(g0_k3), kin_s$h2[1])), isTRUE(all.equal(h2_of(g0_k1), kin_s$h2[2])))
k_at <- function(d, col, g0) c(lo = at_g(d, col, g0 / wrong), true = at_g(d, col, g0),
                              hi = at_g(d, col, g0 * wrong))
k3_cor <- k_at(ek3, "cor", g0_k3); k1_cor <- k_at(ek1, "cor", g0_k1)
k3_topk <- k_at(ek3, "topk", g0_k3); k1_topk <- k_at(ek1, "topk", g0_k1)
k3_loss <- max(k3_cor["true"] - k3_cor[c("lo", "hi")])
k1_loss <- max(k1_cor["true"] - k1_cor[c("lo", "hi")])

# How far REML estimates of gamma wander in the (iid) baseline design: middle 90%.
# Boundary fits have log gamma_hat = -Inf; they are kept (they are estimates
# too) and are fewer than 5%, so both quantiles below are finite.
b_int <- res$baseline$log_gamma_hat
stopifnot(mean(is.infinite(b_int)) < 0.05)
ratio_90 <- exp(quantile(b_int, c(0.05, 0.95)) - log(g0))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(ratio_90)))

# Kinship accuracy at the multiples of the true ratio that bound the middle 90%
# of the baseline estimates.
k3_at90 <- at_g(ek3, "cor", g0_k3 * ratio_90)
iid_at90 <- at_g(ei, "cor", g0 * ratio_90)

# "rankings move" / "many times": the kinship losses are far above the iid loss.
stopifnot(k3_loss > 5 * iid_cor_loss, k1_loss > 5 * iid_cor_loss, k3_loss > sd_cor_base / 2,
          all(k3_cor["true"] - k3_at90 > ei_cor["true"] - iid_at90),
          all(k3_topk[c("lo", "hi")] < k3_topk["true"]),            # top-10% share "falls"
          # realistic errors: "smaller losses than at a factor of 10"
          max(k3_cor["true"] - k3_at90) < min(k3_cor["true"] - k3_cor[c("lo", "hi")]))

# Family structure of G: mean off-diagonal relationship within and between
# the families of make_kinship().
G_kin <- .kinship_G()
fam_kin <- ceiling(seq_len(nrow(G_kin)) * kin_s$n_family / nrow(G_kin))
same_fam <- outer(fam_kin, fam_kin, "==")
G_within <- mean(G_kin[same_fam & row(G_kin) != col(G_kin)])
G_between <- mean(G_kin[!same_fam])

# Robustness checks (scripts/robustness_checks.R): the first trials of the
# kinship experiment, and an uneven-replication design, with BLUPs at the true
# variance ratio, 10 times off, and at the REML estimate.
rob <- res$robust
rob_n <- attr(rob, "n_rep")
rob_mean <- function(chk, col) {
  d <- rob[rob$check == chk & !rob$degenerate, ]
  sapply(c("lo", "true", "hi", "reml"), function(p) mean(d[[col]][d$point == p]))
}
rob_loss <- function(x) max(x["true"] - x[c("lo", "hi")])
rk3 <- lapply(c(all = "cor", within = "cor_within", between = "cor_between"),
              function(col) rob_mean("kinship_0.3", col))
rk1 <- lapply(c(all = "cor", within = "cor_within", between = "cor_between"),
              function(col) rob_mean("kinship_0.1", col))
ru_cor <- rob_mean("uneven", "cor"); rb_cor <- rob_mean("baseline", "cor")
ru_high <- rob_mean("uneven", "n_high_in_top")
ru_loss <- rob_loss(ru_cor); rb_loss <- rob_loss(rb_cor)
ru_reps <- attr(rob, "uneven_rep_counts")
ru_r <- max(ru_reps); ru_n_hi <- sum(ru_reps == ru_r); ru_n_1 <- sum(ru_reps == 1)
ru_n_boundary <- length(unique(rob$rep[rob$check == "uneven" & rob$boundary]))
ru_h2 <- unique(rob$h2[rob$check == "uneven"])
stopifnot(
  all(is.na(rob$error)), attr(rob, "wrong") == wrong,
  isTRUE(all.equal(c(G_within, G_between), c(attr(rob, "G_within"), attr(rob, "G_between")))),
  G_within > 0.3, G_between < 0,                  # "strong family structure"
  # "much of the loss is in ranking genotypes from different families":
  # within families the loss is less than half of the overall loss, and the
  # order of the family means hardly changes.
  rob_loss(rk3$within) < rob_loss(rk3$all) / 2, rob_loss(rk1$within) < rob_loss(rk1$all) / 2,
  rob_loss(rk3$between) < rob_loss(rk3$all) / 2, rob_loss(rk1$between) < rob_loss(rk1$all) / 2,
  # Uneven replication: "several times" the loss of the baseline design, and
  # closer (as a ratio) to the relationship-model loss than to the
  # independent-genotype loss, i.e. "more like the relationship model".
  ru_loss > 3 * rb_loss, ru_loss > 3 * iid_cor_loss, ru_loss^2 > iid_cor_loss * k3_loss,
  # Too small a ratio puts more of the many-plot genotypes in the top 10%,
  # too large a ratio fewer.
  ru_high["lo"] > ru_high["true"], ru_high["true"] > ru_high["hi"],
  # "REML itself ... costs little here"
  ru_cor["true"] - ru_cor["reml"] < ru_loss / 3
)
```

Breeding programs increasingly predict genetic values with a relationship matrix: pedigree-based, or genomic (GBLUP) from markers. To see whether the conclusion survives, we repeated the experiment with genotypes related through a genomic relationship matrix $G$ (VanRaden 2008), at heritabilities `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)` and `r fmt(kin_s$h2[2], 1)`, with `r n_rep` trials each.

<details class="fold">
<summary>How the relationship-model simulation was set up</summary>

We simulated `r length(kin_s$rep_counts)` genotypes from `r kin_s$n_family` families of `r length(kin_s$rep_counts) / kin_s$n_family` and built a genomic relationship matrix $G$ from `r kin_s$n_snp` simulated markers with the method of VanRaden (2008). $G$ was scaled to mean diagonal 1 (plus `r kin_s$ridge` on the diagonal so it can be inverted), so $\sigma^2_g$ is still the genetic variance of a genotype and the heritabilities below are true heritabilities. The genetic values were drawn from $N(0, \sigma^2_g G)$, the field design is the baseline one, and the model is the same as before with $g \sim N(0, \sigma^2_g G)$.

</details>

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
rel_curve <- function(d, label) {
  g0d <- attr(d, "gamma_true")
  d |>
    mutate(ratio = exp(log_gamma) / g0d,
           d_cor = cor - at_g(d, "cor", g0d),
           d_topk = topk - at_g(d, "topk", g0d),
           model = label) |>
    filter(ratio >= 1 / 30, ratio <= 30)
}
rel_df <- bind_rows(
  rel_curve(ei, paste0("Independent genotypes, h² = ", fmt(SETTINGS$baseline$h2, 1))),
  rel_curve(ek3, paste0("Relationship matrix G, h² = ", fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1))),
  rel_curve(ek1, paste0("Relationship matrix G, h² = ", fmt(kin_s$h2[2], 1)))
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model)))
rel_long <- rel_df |>
  select(ratio, model, d_cor, d_topk) |>
  pivot_longer(c(d_cor, d_topk), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric, d_cor = "Change in accuracy, cor(predicted, true)",
                         d_topk = "Change in share of the true top 10% selected"))
ggplot(rel_long, aes(ratio, value, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = col_ink, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1/30, 1/10, 1/3, 1, 3, 10, 30),
                labels = c("1/30", "1/10", "1/3", "1", "3", "10", "30")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_ink, col_main, col_accent), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Average cost of a wrong variance ratio",
       x = "Variance ratio used, as a multiple of the true one",
       y = "Change from the true value") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  my_theme
```

With related genotypes the curves are no longer flat. At $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)`, the average accuracy is `r fmt(k3_cor["true"])` at the true value, `r fmt(k3_cor["lo"])` with a variance ratio `r wrong` times too small and `r fmt(k3_cor["hi"])` with one `r wrong` times too large, and the share of the true top 10% selected falls as well. These losses, up to `r fmt(k3_loss, 3)` at $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)` and `r fmt(k1_loss, 3)` at $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[2], 1)`, are many times the `r fmt(iid_cor_loss, 3)` of the independent-genotype model. With realistic errors instead of a factor of `r wrong` (shown at $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)` in the fold below), the losses are smaller, but still larger than with independent genotypes. This is one genomic $G$ with strong family structure (mean relationship `r fmt(G_within, 2)` within families and `r sub("^-", "&minus;", fmt(G_between, 2))` between them), and much of the loss is in ranking genotypes from different families against each other: within a family the order changed much less.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (top-10% share, families, and realistic errors)</summary>

At $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)` the share of the true top 10% selected falls from `r fmt(k3_topk["true"], 2)` at the true value to `r fmt(k3_topk["lo"], 2)` and `r fmt(k3_topk["hi"], 2)`. At $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[2], 1)` the accuracy goes from `r fmt(k1_cor["true"])` to `r fmt(k1_cor["lo"])` and `r fmt(k1_cor["hi"])`.

A factor of `r wrong` is a large error, so how large are realistic ones? In the baseline design with independent genotypes, the middle 90% of the REML estimates of the variance ratio ranged from `r fmt(ratio_90[1], 2)` to `r fmt(ratio_90[2], 1)` times the true value (Myth 3 looks at this spread). In the relationship model at $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)`, using those two multiples gives an average accuracy of `r fmt(k3_at90[1])` and `r fmt(k3_at90[2])`, against `r fmt(k3_cor["true"])` at the truth: smaller losses than at a factor of `r wrong`, but still larger than in the independent model (`r fmt(iid_at90[1])` and `r fmt(iid_at90[2])` against `r fmt(ei_cor["true"])`).

Where is the loss? We repeated the relationship model on the first `r rob_n` trials at each heritability (`scripts/robustness_checks.R`) and split the accuracy in two: within families (the mean of the `r kin_s$n_family` within-family correlations between predicted and true values) and between families (the correlation between predicted and true family means). At $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[1], 1)`, the overall accuracy on these trials was `r fmt(rk3$all["true"])` at the true value and `r fmt(rk3$all["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk3$all["hi"])` at a ratio `r wrong` times too small and too large. Within families it was `r fmt(rk3$within["true"])`, against `r fmt(rk3$within["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk3$within["hi"])`, and between families `r fmt(rk3$between["true"])`, against `r fmt(rk3$between["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk3$between["hi"])`. At $h^2$ = `r fmt(kin_s$h2[2], 1)`: overall `r fmt(rk1$all["true"])` against `r fmt(rk1$all["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk1$all["hi"])`; within families `r fmt(rk1$within["true"])` against `r fmt(rk1$within["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk1$within["hi"])`; between families `r fmt(rk1$between["true"])` against `r fmt(rk1$between["lo"])` and `r fmt(rk1$between["hi"])`. Neither the order within a family nor the order of the family means moves much. What moves is the weight a genotype's own plots get against its family's mean, and so how genotypes from different families are placed against each other. A relationship matrix with weaker family structure, or a pedigree, may behave differently; we did not simulate one.

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** with a relationship matrix, a genotype's BLUP combines two sources of information: its own plots and the plots of its relatives. The variance ratio decides how much weight each source gets. A genotype with two plots and few close relatives and a genotype with one plot and many close relatives are affected differently when that weight changes, so their order can swap. In the independent model, the only information about a genotype is its own plots (compared with the trial mean), and the variance ratio mostly just scales it.

</div>

**Very uneven replication moves rankings too.** In a trial where `r ru_n_hi` genotypes have `r ru_r` plots and the other `r ru_n_1` one plot each, as in augmented designs or unbalanced multi-environment data, a variance ratio `r wrong` times off cost up to `r fmt(ru_loss, 3)` in average accuracy, several times the `r fmt(iid_cor_loss, 3)` of our baseline design: this behaves more like the relationship model than like the independent model with similar replication. The order among genotypes with the same number of plots does not change at all (they share one shrinkage factor); what moves is how the well-replicated genotypes are placed against the rest, which matters when both are selection candidates rather than checks.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (the uneven-replication check)</summary>

`scripts/robustness_checks.R` simulated `r rob_n` trials with `r ru_n_hi` genotypes in `r ru_r` plots and `r ru_n_1` in one (`r sum(ru_reps)` plots, $h^2$ = `r fmt(ru_h2, 1)`, independent genotypes, otherwise as the baseline design). The average accuracy was `r fmt(ru_cor["true"])` at the true variance ratio, `r fmt(ru_cor["lo"])` with a ratio `r wrong` times too small and `r fmt(ru_cor["hi"])` with one `r wrong` times too large. On the same `r rob_n` seeds the baseline design gave `r fmt(rb_cor["true"])`, `r fmt(rb_cor["lo"])` and `r fmt(rb_cor["hi"])`. At the REML estimate the uneven design averaged `r fmt(ru_cor["reml"])` (leaving out `r ru_n_boundary` boundary `r if (ru_n_boundary == 1) "fit" else "fits"`), so REML itself, landing near the truth on average, costs little here.

The reason is the shrinkage. A genotype with `r ru_r` plots is shrunk little whatever the variance ratio; a genotype with one plot is shrunk a lot, and by how much depends on the ratio. With the ratio too small, the single-plot genotypes are shrunk too hard and the well-replicated ones take more of the top 10%: on average `r fmt(ru_high["lo"], 1)` of the `r k_top` selected, against `r fmt(ru_high["true"], 1)` at the true ratio and `r fmt(ru_high["hi"], 1)` with the ratio too large.

</details>

<div class="takeaway">

**Takeaway for breeders**

- In a simple genotype model where genotypes have similar replication, rankings are robust to where the variance estimate lands: a variance ratio `r wrong` times off cost at most `r fmt(iid_cor_loss, 3)` in average accuracy.
- Heritability, predicted genetic gain and the error of the BLUPs are not robust. They move directly with the estimate.
- With relationships among genotypes (in our simulations, one genomic $G$ with strong family structure), rankings move too: the same error cost up to `r fmt(max(k3_loss, k1_loss), 3)` in accuracy, much of it in ranking genotypes from different families against each other. Very uneven replication moves rankings too (up to `r fmt(ru_loss, 3)`).
- The true variance components give the best predictions on average, but a single trial can do better or worse by luck.

</div>

### Myth 3: All trials are equally trustworthy

```{r, echo=FALSE}
q90 <- function(x) quantile(x, c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
rng_txt <- function(x, d = 2) paste0(fmt(x[1], d), " to ", fmt(x[2], d))
z95 <- qnorm(0.975)

m3 <- lapply(names(designs), function(sc) {
  d <- res[[sc]]
  d <- d[is.na(d$error), ]
  lg0 <- log(SETTINGS[[sc]]$h2 / (1 - SETTINGS[[sc]]$h2))
  interior <- !d$boundary
  # Curvature: only interior fits with a usable (positive) value. The runner
  # already set it to NA at the boundary and where it came out <= 0.
  usable <- interior & is.finite(d$info_log_gamma) & d$info_log_gamma > 0
  se <- d$info_log_gamma[usable]^-0.5
  covered <- abs(d$log_gamma_hat[usable] - lg0) < z95 * se
  # The same curvature on the h2 scale (delta method, exact at the peak):
  # SE(h2) = SE(log gamma) * dh2/dlog gamma = SE(log gamma) * h2 (1 - h2).
  h2u <- d$h2_hat[usable]
  se_h2 <- se * h2u * (1 - h2u)
  h2_0 <- SETTINGS[[sc]]$h2
  covered_h2 <- abs(h2u - h2_0) < z95 * se_h2
  below0 <- h2u - z95 * se_h2 < 0
  # Profile-likelihood intervals for every trial (scripts/profile_coverage.R).
  pc <- res$prof[res$prof$scenario == sc, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(pc) == nrow(d), all(is.na(pc$error)),
            identical(pc$h2_hat, d$h2_hat[match(pc$rep, d$rep)]),
            identical(pc$boundary, d$boundary[match(pc$rep, d$rep)]))
  pc_int <- pc$covered[!pc$boundary]
  list(n_prof = nrow(pc), prof_cover = mean(pc$covered), n_prof_cover = sum(pc$covered),
       prof_cover_int = mean(pc_int), n_prof_int = length(pc_int),
       cover_h2_int = mean(covered_h2), cover_h2_all = sum(covered_h2) / nrow(d),
       n_below0 = sum(below0), p_below0 = mean(below0),
       se_h2_med = median(se_h2), se_h2_90 = q90(se_h2),
       prof_zero = sum(pc$reaches_zero), prof_hi_med = median(pc$h2_hi),
       prof_split = sum(pc$pieces > 1),
       n = nrow(d), n_boundary = sum(d$boundary), n_interior = sum(interior),
       n_unusable = sum(interior & !usable),
       h2_90 = q90(d$h2_hat), gain_90 = q90(d$gain_slope),
       rel_90 = q90(d$reliability), cor_90 = q90(d$cor),
       sd_lg = sd(d$log_gamma_hat[interior]),
       se_med = median(se), se_90 = q90(se),
       cover_int = mean(covered), n_cover = sum(covered), n_usable = sum(usable),
       cover_all = sum(covered) / nrow(d),
       mean_dcor = mean(d$d_cor, na.rm = TRUE))
})
names(m3) <- names(designs)
mw <- m3$weak; mb <- m3$baseline; ms <- m3$strong

# Direction words below; knitting stops if a rerun changes them.
stopifnot(
  diff(mw$h2_90) > diff(ms$h2_90), diff(mb$h2_90) > diff(ms$h2_90),
  diff(mw$gain_90) > diff(mb$gain_90), diff(mb$gain_90) > diff(ms$gain_90),
  abs(ms$se_med / ms$sd_lg - 1) < 0.1,          # strong: curvature matches the spread
  mw$cover_int < mb$cover_int, mb$cover_int < ms$cover_int,
  # Interior fits share one denominator on both scales and for the profile.
  all(sapply(m3, function(s) s$n_prof_int == s$n_usable)),
  # "depend on the scale": in the weak design the two curvature intervals
  # differ in coverage by more than simulation noise (5 points).
  abs(mw$cover_h2_int - mw$cover_int) > 0.05,
  mw$n_boundary > 0,                            # weak: boundary fits "have no interval"
  all(res$prof$h2_lo >= 0),                     # profile: "never goes below zero"
  mw$p_below0 > 0.5,                            # weak, h2 scale: "usually" reaches below zero
  ms$n_below0 == 0,                             # strong: never
  # Profile interval "has none of these problems": above both curvature
  # intervals on all trials and on interior fits in the weak design.
  mw$prof_cover > max(mw$cover_all, mw$cover_h2_all),
  mw$prof_cover_int >= max(mw$cover_int, mw$cover_h2_int),
  abs(ms$cover_h2_int - 0.95) < 0.025,          # strong, h2 scale: "close to the nominal 95%"
  # The log-scale SE swings far more than the h2-scale SE in the weak design.
  mw$se_90[2] / mw$se_90[1] > 5 * mw$se_h2_90[2] / mw$se_h2_90[1],
  mw$se_90[2] / mw$se_90[1] > 5 * ms$se_90[2] / ms$se_90[1],
  diff(sqrt(mw$rel_90)) > diff(mw$cor_90),      # reliability swings more than realized accuracy
  mb$mean_dcor < 0, mw$mean_dcor < 0,           # "lost on average"
  # Profile intervals: at or above nominal, up to simulation noise (binomial
  # 95% CI reaches 0.95), in every design, and clearly better than the
  # curvature intervals (all trials) in the weak and baseline designs.
  all(sapply(m3, `[[`, "prof_cover") > 0.93),
  all(sapply(m3, function(s) binom.test(s$n_prof_cover, s$n_prof)$conf.int[2] >= 0.95)),
  mw$prof_cover - mw$cover_all > 0.2, mb$prof_cover > mb$cover_all,
  mw$prof_cover - mw$cover_h2_all > 0.2, mb$prof_cover > mb$cover_h2_all,
  abs(ms$prof_cover - ms$cover_all) < 0.02,
  all(sapply(m3, `[[`, "prof_split") == 0),
  mw$prof_zero > mw$n / 2,                      # "most weak intervals reach zero"
  all(abs(log(ms$gain_90)) < log(1.25)),        # strong: gain slope "close to 1"
  mw$gain_90[1] < 0.5, mw$gain_90[2] > 2,       # weak: "a large factor in either direction"
  abs(mb$mean_dcor) < 0.005, abs(mw$mean_dcor) < 0.005,   # rankings "pay almost nothing"
  abs(ms$cover_int - 0.95) < 0.025              # strong: "close to the nominal 95%"
)
```

Every number so far came from a single variance estimate per trial. But the hill can be sharp or flat, and that decides how far the estimate wanders from trial to trial. We return to the weak, baseline and strong designs of Myth 1, `r n_rep` trials of each.

#### How far the estimate wanders

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
m3_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(designs), function(sc) {
  res[[sc]] |>
    filter(is.na(error)) |>
    mutate(design = factor(designs[[sc]], levels = designs),
           h2_true = SETTINGS[[sc]]$h2)
}))
lab_df <- data.frame(design = factor(designs, levels = designs),
                     n_b = sapply(m3, `[[`, "n_boundary"))
p_h2 <- ggplot(m3_df, aes(h2_hat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, boundary = 0, fill = col_main, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = h2_true), colour = col_ink, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(data = lab_df, aes(x = 0.6, y = Inf, label = paste0(n_b, " trials at h² = 0")),
            hjust = 1, vjust = 1.5, colour = col_accent, size = 3.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ design, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "REML estimates of heritability", x = expression(hat(h)^2), y = "Trials") +
  my_theme
p_gain <- ggplot(filter(m3_df, !degenerate), aes(design, gain_slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = col_ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = col_main, alpha = 0.3, colour = col_main, outlier.alpha = 0.3,
               width = 0.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Gain slope of the BLUPs", x = NULL, y = "Slope (log scale)") +
  my_theme
p_h2 + p_gain + plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1))
```

In the strong design the hill is sharp: in 90% of the trials the heritability estimate was in the range `r rng_txt(ms$h2_90)` (true value `r fmt(rst$h2, 1)`), and the gain slope stays close to 1. In the weak design, estimates run from `r rng_txt(mw$h2_90)` around a true `r fmt(rw$h2, 1)`, and the gain slope from `r rng_txt(mw$gain_90)`: in a weak trial, the predicted genetic gain can be wrong by a large factor in either direction. The model's own reliability is no safer guide: in the weak design, the accuracy it claims varied more from trial to trial than the realized accuracy did, and it ignores the uncertainty in the variance components themselves (Kackar and Harville 1984).

Among the trials where REML found some genetic variance, rankings pay almost nothing for this wandering, as Myth 2 predicts for independent genotypes with similar replication: compared with BLUPs at the true variance components, the plug-in BLUPs lost on average `r fmt(-mb$mean_dcor, 4)` in accuracy in the baseline design and `r fmt(-mw$mean_dcor, 4)` in the weak design. Boundary fits, which give no ranking at all, are not in that average; we come to them next.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (full table, ranges and caveats)</summary>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
row_m3 <- c(
  "Trials",
  "Estimate at the boundary (genetic variance = 0)",
  "Heritability estimate, middle 90%",
  "Gain slope, middle 90%",
  "Model's own reliability, middle 90%",
  "Realized accuracy, cor(predicted, true), middle 90%",
  "SD of log variance ratio across trials (interior fits)",
  "SE of log variance ratio from the curvature, median (middle 90%)",
  "SE of h² from the curvature, median (middle 90%)",
  "Curvature 95% interval on log variance ratio covers the truth",
  "Curvature 95% interval on h² covers the truth",
  "Curvature interval on h² reaches below 0",
  "Profile-likelihood 95% interval covers the truth",
  "Profile-likelihood interval reaches h² = 0"
)
col_m3 <- function(s) c(
  s$n,
  paste0(s$n_boundary, " (", pct(s$n_boundary / s$n), ")"),
  rng_txt(s$h2_90), rng_txt(s$gain_90), rng_txt(s$rel_90), rng_txt(s$cor_90),
  fmt(s$sd_lg, 2),
  paste0(fmt(s$se_med, 2), " (", rng_txt(s$se_90), ")"),
  paste0(fmt(s$se_h2_med, 2), " (", rng_txt(s$se_h2_90), ")"),
  paste0(pct(s$cover_int), " of ", s$n_usable, " interior fits; ",
         pct(s$cover_all), " of all ", s$n),
  paste0(pct(s$cover_h2_int), " of ", s$n_usable, " interior fits; ",
         pct(s$cover_h2_all), " of all ", s$n),
  paste0(s$n_below0, " of ", s$n_usable, " interior fits"),
  paste0(pct(s$prof_cover_int), " of ", s$n_prof_int, " interior fits; ",
         pct(s$prof_cover), " of all ", s$n_prof),
  paste0(s$prof_zero, " of ", s$n_prof)
)
data.frame(Quantity = row_m3,
           Weak = col_m3(mw), Baseline = col_m3(mb), Strong = col_m3(ms),
           check.names = FALSE) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

In the strong design the gain slope ranged over `r rng_txt(ms$gain_90)` (middle 90%). In the baseline design the middle 90% of heritability estimates spans `r rng_txt(mb$h2_90)` around a true `r fmt(rbase$h2, 1)`, and the gain slope `r rng_txt(mb$gain_90)`. The model's own reliability, computed from the prediction error variances at the estimated variance components, ranged over `r rng_txt(mw$rel_90)` in the weak design, which claims an accuracy (its square root) of `r rng_txt(sqrt(mw$rel_90))`, while the realized accuracy only ranged over `r rng_txt(mw$cor_90)`.

The average loss in accuracy leaves out the boundary fits (`r mb$n_boundary` baseline and `r mw$n_boundary` weak trials). We did not run this replicate study for the relationship model, but its curves in Myth 2 are not flat, so there we would expect the wandering to cost accuracy as well.

</details>

#### Boundary fits: when REML says "no genetic variance"

In `r mw$n_boundary` of the `r mw$n` weak trials (`r pct(mw$n_boundary / mw$n)`), the top of the hill was at $h^2$ = 0: REML set the genetic variance to exactly zero, although every one of those trials was simulated with a true $h^2$ of `r fmt(rw$h2, 1)`. This also happened in `r mb$n_boundary` baseline trials and `r if (ms$n_boundary == 0) "in none of the strong trials" else paste(ms$n_boundary, "strong trials")`. A boundary fit does not mean "there is no genetic variance"; it means this trial cannot tell the genetic variance apart from zero. The consequences are severe: every BLUP is zero, so the model ranks nothing, and a reported heritability of zero says nothing about how large the genetic variance could be (the profile-likelihood interval below does). If the entries of such a trial must still be ranked, the usual fallback is to fit genotype as a fixed effect and rank its estimated means (BLUEs). Count boundary fits and report them. They say this trial could not separate genetic variance from noise, not that genetic variance is absent.

#### The width of the hill

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Hills of the first trial (replicate 1) of each design: curvature-based
# (Wald) interval vs profile-likelihood interval, both nominal 95%.
hill_one <- function(sc) {
  s <- SETTINGS[[sc]]
  seed <- BASE_SEED + 1
  des <- make_design(s$rep_counts, seed = seed)
  sim <- simulate_trial(des, h2 = s$h2, seed = seed)
  dm <- design_matrices(des)
  su <- reml_setup(sim$y, dm$X, dm$Z)
  fit <- reml_fit(su)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fit$loglik, res[[sc]]$loglik_max[1], tolerance = 1e-8)))
  h2g <- seq(0, 0.98, by = 0.002)
  ll <- reml_loglik(h2g / (1 - h2g), su) - fit$loglik
  inside <- h2g[ll >= -drop_95]
  se <- fit$info_log_gamma^-0.5
  w <- exp(log(fit$gamma) + c(-1, 1) * z95 * se)
  list(curve = data.frame(design = designs[[sc]], h2 = h2g, ll = ll),
       h2_hat = fit$h2, h2_true = s$h2, boundary = fit$boundary,
       prof = range(inside), wald = h2_of(w),
       wald_h2 = fit$h2 + c(-1, 1) * z95 * se * fit$h2 * (1 - fit$h2), ll0 = ll[1])
}
hills <- lapply(setNames(names(designs), names(designs)), hill_one)
stopifnot(!any(sapply(hills, `[[`, "boundary")))
hw <- hills$weak; hs <- hills$strong
inside_iv <- function(iv, x) iv[1] <= x && x <= iv[2]
stopifnot(max(abs(hs$prof - hs$wald)) < 0.02,   # strong: "almost coincide"
          max(abs(hs$prof - hs$wald_h2)) < 0.02,
          max(abs(hw$prof - hw$wald)) > 0.03,   # weak: "they disagree"
          max(abs(hw$prof - hw$wald_h2)) > 0.03)
# Which of the weak trial's three intervals contain the true value.
hw_in <- c(profile = inside_iv(hw$prof, hw$h2_true), log = inside_iv(hw$wald, hw$h2_true),
           h2 = inside_iv(hw$wald_h2, hw$h2_true))
stopifnot(any(hw_in))
```

How sharp is the hill? The standard answer is its *curvature* at the peak. The standard errors that mixed-model software reports for variance components come from this kind of curvature (the information matrix), and the usual "estimate ± 2 SE" interval assumes the hill is shaped like an upside-down parabola *on the scale where the SE was computed*. The same curvature gives different intervals on different scales, so we built it on two: the log of the variance ratio, $\log\gamma$, and $h^2$ itself, the scale a breeder reports.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Under the hood: curvature-based and profile-likelihood intervals</summary>

On the scale of $\log\gamma$, the observed information is the curvature of the profile log-likelihood at its peak, $J = -\partial^2 \ell / \partial(\log\gamma)^2$, and the curvature-based standard error is $\text{SE}(\log\hat\gamma) \approx J^{-1/2}$. The curvature-based 95% interval on that scale is $\log\hat\gamma \pm `r fmt(z95, 2)`\,J^{-1/2}$, which, mapped to $h^2$, is lopsided and never reaches below zero. On the $h^2$ scale, with $h^2 = \gamma/(1+\gamma)$ and so $dh^2/d\log\gamma = h^2(1-h^2)$, the same curvature gives $\text{SE}(\hat h^2) \approx \hat h^2(1-\hat h^2)\,J^{-1/2}$ (the delta method, exact for the curvature at the peak) and the symmetric interval $\hat h^2 \pm `r fmt(z95, 2)`\,\text{SE}(\hat h^2)$, which can. Software often reports the SE of $\hat\sigma^2_g$ itself, a third scale. At a boundary fit there is no curvature at the peak, so neither interval exists. The profile-likelihood interval instead keeps every value whose log-likelihood is within `r fmt(drop_95, 2)` units of the peak (half the 95% quantile of $\chi^2_1$), the shaded band of the first hill figure. The profile interval is the same on every scale. The intervals agree when the hill really is a parabola, which happens when the data carry a lot of information. Near the boundary, the `r fmt(drop_95, 2)`-unit rule is itself only approximate (the same boundary issue as the LRT), but unlike the curvature it lets the interval reach zero. We check how well each interval actually covers the truth below.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>A closer look: the three intervals on one trial of each design</summary>

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=11, fig.height=4.2, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
hill_df <- bind_rows(lapply(hills, `[[`, "curve")) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = designs)) |>
  filter(ll >= -8)
iv_types <- c("Profile likelihood", "Curvature on log γ (± 1.96 SE)",
              "Curvature on h² (± 1.96 SE)")
int_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(hills), function(sc) {
  h <- hills[[sc]]
  data.frame(design = designs[[sc]], type = iv_types,
             lo = c(h$prof[1], h$wald[1], h$wald_h2[1]),
             hi = c(h$prof[2], h$wald[2], h$wald_h2[2]),
             y = c(-6.2, -7.1, -8.0))
})) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = designs),
         type = factor(type, levels = iv_types))
x_min <- min(0, int_df$lo) - 0.02
true_df <- data.frame(design = factor(designs, levels = designs),
                      h2 = sapply(hills, `[[`, "h2_true"))
ggplot(hill_df, aes(h2, ll)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -drop_95, colour = col_ink, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(data = true_df, aes(xintercept = h2), colour = col_ink, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = col_main, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_segment(data = int_df, aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = y, yend = y, colour = type),
               linewidth = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_accent, col_third, col_ink), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ design) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(x_min, 0.9)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  labs(title = "The first trial of each design: profile vs curvature intervals",
       x = expression(h^2), y = "Log-likelihood below the peak") +
  my_theme
```

These are the first simulated trials of each design (no selection). In the strong trial the three intervals almost coincide: `r rng_txt(hs$prof)` from the profile likelihood, `r rng_txt(hs$wald)` from the curvature on $\log\gamma$ and `r rng_txt(hs$wald_h2)` from the curvature on $h^2$. In the weak trial the hill is flat and lopsided, and they disagree: `r rng_txt(hw$prof)` from the profile, `r rng_txt(hw$wald)` on $\log\gamma$ and `r rng_txt(hw$wald_h2)` on $h^2$. `r if (hw_in[["profile"]] && !hw_in[["log"]] && !hw_in[["h2"]]) paste0("In this one trial only the profile interval contains the true value, ", fmt(hw$h2_true, 1), "; one trial proves little, and the coverage over all trials is below.") else paste0("The true value, ", fmt(hw$h2_true, 1), ", is inside ", paste(c("the profile interval", "the log-scale interval", "the h² interval")[hw_in], collapse = " and "), " in this one trial; the coverage over all trials is below.")`

</details>
