Across all trials, the curvature works in the strong design: its median standard error of $\log\hat\gamma$, `r fmt(ms$se_med, 2)`, matches the actual spread of the estimates across trials (standard deviation `r fmt(ms$sd_lg, 2)`), and the curvature-based interval covered the true value in `r pct(ms$cover_int)` of the trials on the $\log\gamma$ scale and `r pct(ms$cover_h2_int)` on the $h^2$ scale, close to the nominal 95%. In the weak design three things go wrong:

- **The interval depends on the scale.** Among the interior fits, it covered the true value in `r pct(mw$cover_int)` of trials on the $\log\gamma$ scale and `r pct(mw$cover_h2_int)` on the $h^2$ scale.
- **Boundary fits have no interval.** In `r pct(mw$n_boundary / mw$n)` of the weak trials the peak is at zero, with no curvature to use.
- **On the $h^2$ scale it usually reaches below zero**, into heritabilities that cannot exist: `r pct(mw$p_below0)` of the interior fits. Truncating it at zero keeps its coverage (still `r pct(mw$cover_h2_int)` of interior fits here, since the true value is above zero), but the interval is then no longer the symmetric one the standard error describes.

The 95% profile-likelihood interval has none of these problems: it is the same on every scale, it exists for every trial, boundary fits included, and it never goes below zero. It covered the true value in `r pct(mw$prof_cover)` of all weak trials, `r pct(mb$prof_cover)` of the baseline trials and `r pct(ms$prof_cover)` of the strong trials. In the weak design it does so by being honest rather than precise: `r mw$prof_zero` of the `r mw$n_prof` weak intervals reach $h^2$ = 0. A profile interval does not make a weak trial informative; it tells you how little the trial knows. That makes it the better interval to report (on profile-likelihood intervals in general, see Pawitan 2001), and it needs nothing more than the log-likelihood evaluated at a range of variance ratios.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (coverage, counts and how the intervals were computed)</summary>

Coverage of the nominal 95% intervals, first over the interior fits (where all three exist) and then over all trials, counting a boundary fit as a miss for the curvature intervals, which do not exist there:

- **Weak** (`r mw$n_usable` interior fits of `r mw$n`): $\log\gamma$ scale `r pct(mw$cover_int)`, $h^2$ scale `r pct(mw$cover_h2_int)`, profile `r pct(mw$prof_cover_int)`; over all trials `r pct(mw$cover_all)`, `r pct(mw$cover_h2_all)` and `r pct(mw$prof_cover)`.
- **Baseline** (`r mb$n_usable` of `r mb$n`): `r pct(mb$cover_int)`, `r pct(mb$cover_h2_int)` and `r pct(mb$prof_cover_int)`; over all trials `r pct(mb$cover_all)`, `r pct(mb$cover_h2_all)` and `r pct(mb$prof_cover)`.
- **Strong** (`r ms$n_usable` of `r ms$n`): `r pct(ms$cover_int)`, `r pct(ms$cover_h2_int)` and `r pct(ms$prof_cover_int)`; over all trials `r pct(ms$cover_all)`, `r pct(ms$cover_h2_all)` and `r pct(ms$prof_cover)`.

How precise a weak trial looks also depends on the scale. Among its `r mw$n_usable` interior fits, the standard error of $\log\hat\gamma$ ranged from `r rng_txt(mw$se_90)` (middle 90%): near the boundary the hill is almost flat in $\log\gamma$. The standard error of $\hat h^2$ only ranged from `r rng_txt(mw$se_h2_90)`, but `r mw$n_below0` of those `r mw$n_usable` $h^2$ intervals (`r pct(mw$p_below0)`) reached below zero, against `r mb$n_below0` of `r mb$n_usable` in the baseline design and `r ms$n_below0` in the strong one.`r if (mw$n_unusable > 0) paste0(" A further ", mw$n_unusable, " interior fits had a non-positive curvature and are left out.") else ""`

The profile-likelihood intervals were computed by `scripts/profile_coverage.R`, for every one of the `r n_rep` trials of each design; the interval runs down to zero when the log-likelihood at zero genetic variance is within `r fmt(drop_95, 2)` units of the peak. The median upper end of the weak intervals is $h^2$ = `r fmt(mw$prof_hi_med, 2)`.

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** a trial with little information gives a flat hill. Its peak can land almost anywhere, including at zero, and the standard error printed next to the estimate cannot tell you that: it is computed from the shape of the hill right at the peak, it gives a different interval on each scale, and at zero it does not exist. Look at the whole hill instead.

</div>

<div class="takeaway">

**Takeaway for breeders**

- The same design can give very different variance estimates from trial to trial. In our weak design, the heritability estimates ranged from `r rng_txt(mw$h2_90)` (middle 90%) around a true `r fmt(rw$h2, 1)`, and `r pct(mw$n_boundary / mw$n)` of the trials estimated it as zero.
- Heritability, predicted gain and reliability from a weak trial are unreliable; rankings from a simple genotype model with similar replication are much less affected.
- Count and report boundary fits ($\hat\sigma^2_g$ = 0). They say this trial could not separate genetic variance from noise, not that genetic variance is absent.
- Intervals from standard errors of variance components (the curvature at the peak) are fine in informative trials. In weak trials they depend on the scale they are built on, do not exist for boundary fits and, on the $h^2$ scale, usually reach below zero. Profile-likelihood intervals have none of these problems, and were at or above their nominal 95% coverage, up to simulation noise, in all three of our designs (`r pct(min(sapply(m3, "[[", "prof_cover")))` to `r pct(max(sapply(m3, "[[", "prof_cover")))`); in weak trials they are wide, and that width is the honest answer.

</div>

### Myth 4: "Not converged" is just a warning

Back to the message from the introduction. Like most mixed-model software, ASReml finds the top of the hill by climbing it step by step, with the *average information* (AI) algorithm of Gilmour, Thompson and Cullis (1995): each step uses the slope of the log-likelihood and an approximation to its curvature to jump towards the peak. The program stops when the log-likelihood and the variance components stop changing. If it reaches its iteration limit first, it prints the warning and returns wherever it got to.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# The same poor start as the convergence experiment (R/experiments.R).
poor_start <- c(genotype = 0.001, residual = 10)
```

To see what that means, we wrote a small AI-REML solver in base R (`R/ai_reml.R` in the repository) that behaves the same way, warnings included. Here it is on the trial of the hill figure, started from a poor guess (genetic variance `r poor_start[["genotype"]]`, residual variance `r poor_start[["residual"]]`, as can happen when starting values are carried over from another trait or scale) and allowed only two iterations:

```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
effects <- list(genotype = list(Z = dm_1$Z, G = NULL))
fit_short <- ai_reml(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, effects,
                     start = c(genotype = 0.001, residual = 10), maxit = 2)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
fit_full <- suppressWarnings(ai_reml(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, effects, start = poor_start))
stopifnot(!fit_short$converged, fit_full$converged,
          abs(fit_full$loglik - fit_1$loglik) < 1e-4)
one_fit_row <- function(f) {
  s2 <- f$sigma2
  g_hat <- blup(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z, s2[["genotype"]] / s2[["residual"]])$g
  acc <- accuracy_metrics(g_hat, sim_1$g, g_hat)
  c(Iterations = f$iterations,
    Converged = if (f$converged) "yes" else "no",
    `Log-likelihood` = fmt(f$loglik, 2),
    `Genetic variance` = fmt(s2[["genotype"]], 3),
    `Residual variance` = fmt(s2[["residual"]], 3),
    `Heritability` = fmt(s2[["genotype"]] / sum(s2), 3),
    `Accuracy, cor(predicted, true)` = fmt(acc$cor, 3),
    `True top 10% selected` = paste0(round(acc$topk * k_top), " of ", k_top))
}
# "Its accuracy moved much less" than the heritability (relative change).
short_h2 <- fit_short$sigma2[["genotype"]] / sum(fit_short$sigma2)
full_h2 <- fit_full$sigma2[["genotype"]] / sum(fit_full$sigma2)
short_cor <- with(fit_short, accuracy_metrics(
  blup(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z, sigma2[["genotype"]] / sigma2[["residual"]])$g, sim_1$g, sim_1$g)$cor)
full_cor <- with(fit_full, accuracy_metrics(
  blup(sim_1$y, dm_1$X, dm_1$Z, sigma2[["genotype"]] / sigma2[["residual"]])$g, sim_1$g, sim_1$g)$cor)
stopifnot(abs(short_cor / full_cor - 1) < abs(short_h2 / full_h2 - 1) / 10,
          fit_full$loglik > fit_short$loglik)   # "below the maximum"
```

The unconverged fit reports a log-likelihood `r fmt(fit_full$loglik - fit_short$loglik, 1)` units below the maximum and a heritability of `r fmt(fit_short$sigma2[["genotype"]] / sum(fit_short$sigma2), 2)` instead of `r fmt(fit_full$sigma2[["genotype"]] / sum(fit_full$sigma2), 2)`. Its accuracy moved much less, from `r fmt(full_cor, 3)` at convergence to `r fmt(short_cor, 3)`. The log-likelihood our solver reports is the honest one at the point where it stopped, not the maximum.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The two fits side by side</summary>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
data.frame(rbind(`Stopped at the limit` = one_fit_row(fit_short),
                 `Run to convergence` = one_fit_row(fit_full)),
           check.names = FALSE) |>
  kable(align = "r")
```

</details>

#### Across `r n_rep` trials

```{r, echo=FALSE}
conv <- res$conv |> filter(is.na(error))
ref <- conv |> filter(start == "default", maxit == max(maxit)) |>
  select(rep, h2_ref = h2, cor_ref = cor)
conv_tbl <- conv |>
  left_join(ref, by = "rep") |>
  group_by(start, maxit) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            conv = mean(converged),
            gap_med = median(loglik_gap),
            h2_lo = quantile(h2, 0.05), h2_hi = quantile(h2, 0.95),
            dh2_med = median(abs(h2 - h2_ref)),
            cor_mean = mean(cor),
            dcor_med = median(abs(cor - cor_ref)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(start = factor(start, levels = c("default", "poor"))) |>
  arrange(start, maxit)
cv_max <- max(conv$maxit)
c_def1 <- filter(conv_tbl, start == "default", maxit == 1)
c_poor <- filter(conv_tbl, start == "poor", maxit < cv_max)
c_ref <- filter(conv_tbl, start == "default", maxit == cv_max)
worst_cor_shift <- max(abs(conv_tbl$cor_mean - c_ref$cor_mean))
# Baseline trials whose REML maximum is at zero genetic variance: the solver
# stops at its lower bound (1e-8 x var(y)), so its BLUPs are tiny but not all
# equal and their accuracy is defined.
conv_bnd <- filter(conv, rep %in% res$baseline$rep[res$baseline$boundary], maxit == cv_max)
stopifnot(length(unique(conv_bnd$rep)) == mb$n_boundary, all(conv_bnd$h2 < 1e-6),
          !anyNA(conv_bnd$cor))
stopifnot(
  length(unique(conv$rep)) == n_rep,
  all(conv$loglik_gap < 1e-6),                       # never above the maximum
  all(filter(conv_tbl, maxit == cv_max)$conv == 1),  # all runs converge with enough iterations
  worst_cor_shift < 0.005,                           # "mean accuracy barely moves"
  all(c_poor$gap_med < -2 * LRT_CRIT),               # gaps larger than the LRT cutoff
  all(abs(filter(conv, maxit == cv_max)$loglik_gap) < 1e-6),   # "to the same maximum"
  -c_def1$gap_med < min(-c_poor$gap_med) / 10,       # sensible start "much more forgiving"
  c_def1$dh2_med < min(c_poor$dh2_med)
)
```

We ran the solver on all `r n_rep` baseline trials from two starting points, a *sensible* one that splits the variance of the data equally between genotype and residual and the *poor* one above, with iteration limits of `r paste(sort(unique(conv$maxit)), collapse = ", ")`. With `r cv_max` iterations every run converged, from either start, to the same maximum the oracle finds.

- **The accuracy hardly moves.** Even the runs stopped after one step from the poor start predicted with a mean accuracy of `r fmt(filter(c_poor, maxit == 1)$cor_mean, 3)`, against `r fmt(c_ref$cor_mean, 3)` at convergence. That matches Myth 2: in this model the rankings barely depend on the variance estimate. (These means include the `r mb$n_boundary` boundary trials; see the fold below.)
- **Everything else moves.** From the poor start, the median log-likelihood after `r paste(c_poor$maxit, collapse = ", ")` iterations was `r paste(fmt(-c_poor$gap_med, 1), collapse = ", ")` units below the maximum. Any likelihood-ratio test built from such a value is off by twice that, far more than the `r fmt(LRT_CRIT, 2)` cutoff of a 5% test. The heritability is off by a median of `r paste(fmt(c_poor$dh2_med, 2), collapse = ", ")`, and its value depends on where the solver started and when it was stopped.
- **A sensible start is much more forgiving.** After a single step from the sensible start the median gap was `r fmt(-c_def1$gap_med, 2)` units and the heritability was off by a median of `r fmt(c_def1$dh2_med, 3)`. That is close, but the program cannot tell you from the warning alone which situation you are in.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (all starts and iteration limits)</summary>

"Off by" compares each run with the converged fit on the same trial. Across all rows of the table the mean accuracy differs by at most `r fmt(worst_cor_shift, 4)`.

The `r mb$n_boundary` baseline trials whose REML maximum is at zero genetic variance are included here. The solver cannot reach zero: it stops at its lower bound, a genetic variance of 10<sup>-8</sup> times the variance of the data ($h^2$ = `r sci(max(conv_bnd$h2))`), where the BLUPs are tiny but not all equal, so their accuracy is defined. Myths 1 and 3 treat the same trials as boundary fits with no accuracy.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
data.frame(
  Start = ifelse(conv_tbl$start == "default", "Sensible", "Poor"),
  `Iteration limit` = conv_tbl$maxit,
  Converged = pct(conv_tbl$conv, 0),
  `Log-lik below maximum (median)` = fmt(-conv_tbl$gap_med, 3),
  `Heritability, middle 90%` = paste0(fmt(conv_tbl$h2_lo, 2), " to ", fmt(conv_tbl$h2_hi, 2)),
  `Heritability off by (median)` = fmt(conv_tbl$dh2_med, 3),
  `Mean accuracy` = fmt(conv_tbl$cor_mean, 3),
  `Accuracy off by (median)` = fmt(conv_tbl$dcor_med, 4),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

</details>

#### What the theory does and does not promise

The textbook guarantees (a consistent estimate, standard errors from the information matrix, known distributions for likelihood-ratio tests) are for the REML *maximum*. A run that stops at an iteration limit from an arbitrary start is a different estimator, defined by the start and the limit, with no such guarantee.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The fine print: what the theory promises, and when one step is enough</summary>

The guarantees in the textbooks are for the REML *maximum*: under normality and regularity conditions (enough levels, true values away from the boundary), the maximizer is consistent and approximately normal, with standard errors from the information matrix (Cressie and Lahiri 1993; Jiang 1996), and likelihood-ratio tests between converged fits have known large-sample distributions, even when the true value of a variance is on the boundary (Self and Liang 1987; Stram and Lee 1994). Strictly, the maximum is not the only estimator with such guarantees: a single Newton-type step from a $\sqrt{n}$-consistent starting value, one whose error already shrinks as fast as that of the estimator itself, is asymptotically as good as the maximum (the one-step estimator; Lehmann and Casella 1998). Our sensible start, half the variance of the data for each component, is not such a value: it is a fixed 50:50 split, not a consistent estimate of either component. A start that is already near the peak behaves similarly in practice, which is what the table shows, but default starting values carry no such guarantee, and a run that stops at an iteration limit from an arbitrary start is a different estimator, defined by the start and the limit, with no guarantee at all.

</details>

<div class="plainwords">

**In plain words:** "Log-likelihood not converged" is not mainly a warning about your BLUPs; in a simple genotype model they are usually fine. It is a warning about every number that is supposed to come from the *top* of the hill: the log-likelihood, likelihood-ratio tests, AIC or BIC, variance components, heritability and their standard errors. Those are reported from wherever the climb stopped.

</div>

<div class="takeaway">

**Takeaway for breeders**

- An unconverged fit can give nearly the same rankings as a converged one, and still report a wrong log-likelihood, wrong variance components and a wrong heritability.
- Never compare log-likelihoods, run likelihood-ratio tests or report heritability from a fit that has not converged. Run it to convergence (more iterations, better starting values), and check that different starts reach the same maximum.
- Convergence is about the *validity* of the reported numbers, not a guarantee of more accurate predictions.

</div>

### Checking predictions: cross-validation

```{r, echo=FALSE}
pick_stats <- function(d) {
  d <- d[is.na(d$error), ]
  both_ok <- !d$degenerate_A & !d$degenerate_B
  # The analysts' predictions differ only when A's extra variance is above
  # zero; otherwise the two models coincide and their accuracies differ only
  # by rounding, so there is no "more accurate analyst" to pick.
  differ <- both_ok & d$sigma2_extra_hat > 0
  stopifnot(all(d$cor_A[differ] != d$cor_B[differ]))
  a_better <- d$cor_A > d$cor_B
  rules <- list(
    `Higher log-likelihood` = d$loglik_A - d$loglik_B > LOGLIK_TOL,
    `Likelihood-ratio test at 5%` = d$lrt > LRT_CRIT,
    `Cross-validation (lower prediction error)` = d$cv_mse_A < d$cv_mse_B
  )
  # Reference rules that ignore the data.
  rules$`Always B (simpler model)` <- rep(FALSE, nrow(d))
  rules$`Always A (larger model)` <- rep(TRUE, nrow(d))
  out <- lapply(rules, function(pick_A) {
    right <- pick_A[differ] == a_better[differ]
    ci <- binom.test(sum(right), length(right))$conf.int
    list(p = mean(right), lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2],
         acc = mean(ifelse(pick_A, d$cor_A, d$cor_B)[both_ok]),
         pick_A = mean(pick_A[differ]),
         # Conditional pick rates: P(picks A | A more accurate), P(picks A | B more accurate).
         k_if_A = sum(pick_A[differ & a_better]), n_if_A = sum(differ & a_better),
         k_if_B = sum(pick_A[differ & !a_better]), n_if_B = sum(differ & !a_better))
  })
  list(rules = out, n_differ = sum(differ), n_ok = sum(both_ok),
       n_same = sum(both_ok & d$sigma2_extra_hat == 0),
       max_same = max(abs(d$cor_A - d$cor_B)[both_ok & d$sigma2_extra_hat == 0], 0),
       a_better = mean(a_better[differ]),
       acc_A = mean(d$cor_A[both_ok]), acc_B = mean(d$cor_B[both_ok]),
       cv_ties = sum(d$cv_mse_A == d$cv_mse_B))
}
ps <- pick_stats(res$spurious)
pr <- pick_stats(res$real)
r_ll <- "Higher log-likelihood"; r_lrt <- "Likelihood-ratio test at 5%"
r_cv <- "Cross-validation (lower prediction error)"
r_B <- "Always B (simpler model)"; r_A <- "Always A (larger model)"
pp <- function(x) paste0(pct(x$p), " (", fmt(100 * x$lo, 0), " to ", fmt(100 * x$hi, 0), "%)")
cond_txt <- function(x) paste0(x$k_if_A, " of ", x$n_if_A, " (", pct(x$k_if_A / x$n_if_A, 0),
                               ") where A was more accurate and ", x$k_if_B, " of ", x$n_if_B,
                               " (", pct(x$k_if_B / x$n_if_B, 0), ") where B was")
pa <- function(x, rule) x$rules[[rule]]$k_if_A / x$rules[[rule]]$n_if_A
pb <- function(x, rule) x$rules[[rule]]$k_if_B / x$rules[[rule]]$n_if_B

# Direction words below; knitting stops if a rerun changes them.
stopifnot(
  ps$rules[[r_cv]]$p > ps$rules[[r_ll]]$p,     # spurious: CV beats "higher logL"
  ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$p > ps$rules[[r_ll]]$p,    # spurious: LRT beats "higher logL"
  pr$rules[[r_ll]]$p > pr$rules[[r_cv]]$p,     # real: "higher logL" beats CV
  ps$rules[[r_cv]]$acc > ps$rules[[r_ll]]$acc,
  ps$acc_B > ps$acc_A, pr$acc_A > pr$acc_B,
  # "about as well": LRT better when spurious, within a point when real
  ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$p > ps$rules[[r_cv]]$p,
  abs(pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$p - pr$rules[[r_cv]]$p) < 0.01,
  # No data-driven rule beat the reference rule that matches the world.
  ps$rules[[r_B]]$p > max(sapply(ps$rules[c(r_ll, r_lrt, r_cv)], `[[`, "p")),
  pr$rules[[r_A]]$p >= max(sapply(pr$rules[c(r_ll, r_lrt, r_cv)], `[[`, "p")),
  ps$rules[[r_B]]$acc > max(sapply(ps$rules[c(r_ll, r_lrt, r_cv)], `[[`, "acc")),
  # CV and LRT pick A far more often when the term is real (a signal across worlds) ...
  pr$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A - ps$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A > 0.3,
  pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$pick_A - ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$pick_A > 0.3,
  # ... but within a world they do not pick A more often when A is the better model.
  pa(ps, r_cv) <= pb(ps, r_cv), pa(ps, r_lrt) <= pb(ps, r_lrt),
  pa(pr, r_cv) <= pb(pr, r_cv), pa(pr, r_lrt) <= pb(pr, r_lrt),
  # CV adopts the spurious term less often than "higher log-likelihood".
  ps$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A < ps$rules[[r_ll]]$pick_A,
  # "protect you from adopting a spurious term most of the time"
  ps$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A < 0.5, ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$pick_A < 0.5,
  # real: "higher log-likelihood" is the same as always choosing the larger model
  isTRUE(all.equal(pr$rules[[r_ll]]$p, pr$rules[[r_A]]$p)),
  # "picks A in essentially every trial" / "almost always says A"
  ps$rules[[r_ll]]$pick_A > 0.95, pr$rules[[r_ll]]$pick_A > 0.95,
  # real: CV and the LRT "give up some of those trials"
  pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$p < pr$rules[[r_ll]]$p,
  # "On individual trials, like the one in the introduction, the difference can be much larger"
  hook$cor_B - hook$cor_A > 2 * max(diff(range(sapply(ps$rules, `[[`, "acc"))),
                                    diff(range(sapply(pr$rules, `[[`, "acc"))))
)
```

In a real trial nobody knows the true genetic values, so nobody can compute the accuracies in our tables. What a breeder can do is check how well each model predicts data it has not seen. We did this for the two analysts with `r SETTINGS$cv_folds`-fold cross-validation over held-out plots, and picked the analyst with the lower cross-validation error.

<details class="fold">
<summary>How the cross-validation was done</summary>

The plots of each trial were split at random into `r SETTINGS$cv_folds` groups (a new split for every trial, the same split for both analysts). Each analyst refitted their model, with REML, on `r SETTINGS$cv_folds - 1` groups and predicted the plots of the remaining group from the fitted mean and the predicted effects, and we averaged the squared prediction errors over all plots. A genotype whose only plot is held out is predicted from the mean, plus its family or block effect for Analyst A.

</details>

We compare three rules for choosing between the analysts: pick A when A's log-likelihood is higher, when the likelihood-ratio test is significant at 5%, or when A's cross-validation error is lower; otherwise pick B. A rule is right when it picks the analyst whose predictions were more accurate, which is defined only when A's extra variance is estimated above zero (otherwise the two models coincide).

- **When the family effect is spurious**, "higher log-likelihood" picks A in essentially every trial where A's extra variance is above zero, so it is right only when A happens to be more accurate: `r pct(ps$rules[[r_ll]]$p)` of the time. Cross-validation was right in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_cv]]$p)` of the trials and the likelihood-ratio test in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$p)`. But simply always keeping the simpler model was right in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_B]]$p)`, more than any rule that looks at the data, and gave the highest mean accuracy (`r fmt(ps$rules[[r_B]]$acc)`).
- **When the block effect is real**, A is the more accurate analyst in `r pct(pr$a_better)` of the trials, so "higher log-likelihood", which almost always says A, is right `r pct(pr$rules[[r_ll]]$p)` of the time, the same as always choosing the larger model. Cross-validation (`r pct(pr$rules[[r_cv]]$p)`) and the likelihood-ratio test (`r pct(pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$p)`) give up some of those trials.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (full table, intervals and counts)</summary>

"Higher" means that A's log-likelihood exceeds B's by more than `r sci(LOGLIK_TOL)`. The analysts' predictions differ, and both are defined, in `r ps$n_differ` spurious-family trials and `r pr$n_differ` real-block trials. In the other `r ps$n_same` spurious-family trials with defined predictions, A's model collapsed to B's and the two accuracies were equal up to rounding (at most `r sci(ps$max_same)` apart).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
rule_names <- names(ps$rules)
data.frame(
  Rule = rule_names,
  `Spurious: picks A` = sapply(ps$rules, function(x) pct(x$pick_A)),
  `Spurious: picks the more accurate analyst` = sapply(ps$rules, pp),
  `Spurious: mean accuracy` = sapply(ps$rules, function(x) fmt(x$acc)),
  `Real: picks A` = sapply(pr$rules, function(x) pct(x$pick_A)),
  `Real: picks the more accurate analyst` = sapply(pr$rules, pp),
  `Real: mean accuracy` = sapply(pr$rules, function(x) fmt(x$acc)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

"Picks A" and "picks the more accurate analyst" are over the `r ps$n_differ` (spurious) and `r pr$n_differ` (real) trials where the analysts differ, the latter with 95% confidence intervals. Mean accuracies are of the predictions each rule chooses, over all trials where both predictions are defined (`r ps$n_ok` and `r pr$n_ok`). The last two rows ignore the data and are there for reference.

</details>

So what do cross-validation and the test actually detect? In the trials where the analysts differ, cross-validation chose A in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A)` of the spurious-family trials and `r pct(pr$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A)` of the real-block trials; the test in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$pick_A)` and `r pct(pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$pick_A)`. They clearly respond to whether the extra term is real. Within one world, though, they do not tell you which analyst will predict better on the trial in front of you: neither chose A more often when A was actually the better model.

<details class="fold">
<summary>The numbers behind this (how often each rule chose A)</summary>

In the spurious-family world, cross-validation chose A in `r cond_txt(ps$rules[[r_cv]])`; the test chose A in `r cond_txt(ps$rules[[r_lrt]])`. In the real-block world, cross-validation chose A in `r cond_txt(pr$rules[[r_cv]])`, and the test in `r cond_txt(pr$rules[[r_lrt]])`.

</details>

The honest summary:

- "Higher log-likelihood" is not a decision rule. It says "A" almost every time A's extra variance is above zero, whether or not the term is real.
- Cross-validation and the likelihood-ratio test detect whether the extra term is real: a signal about the population of trials, not about which model wins on this one. Used that way, they protect you from adopting a spurious term most of the time (cross-validation adopted it in `r pct(ps$rules[[r_cv]]$pick_A)` of the trials where its variance was above zero, against `r pct(ps$rules[[r_ll]]$pick_A)` for "higher log-likelihood"), at some cost when the term is real.
- For a nested random term like these, the test did about as well as cross-validation: better when the term was spurious (`r pct(ps$rules[[r_lrt]]$p)` against `r pct(ps$rules[[r_cv]]$p)`), within a point when it was real (`r pct(pr$rules[[r_lrt]]$p)` against `r pct(pr$rules[[r_cv]]$p)`).
- In accuracy terms the stakes per trial are modest on average in this design: the mean accuracies of the five rules lie within `r fmt(diff(range(sapply(ps$rules, "[[", "acc"))), 3)` of each other in the spurious-family world and within `r fmt(diff(range(sapply(pr$rules, "[[", "acc"))), 3)` in the real-block world. On individual trials, like the one in the introduction, the difference can be much larger.
- Cross-validation's real advantage is that it can be applied where the test cannot: comparing models that are not nested, or models with different fixed effects or relationship matrices.

<details class="fold">
<summary>Caveats about cross-validation</summary>

- Cross-validation over held-out plots measures how well a model predicts *plot values*, which include field effects, not genetic values directly. If the goal is to predict new genotypes, hold out genotypes instead (all plots of a genotype in the same group).
- A single `r SETTINGS$cv_folds`-fold split is noisy. Repeating the split several times and averaging is cheap and steadier (we did not test this here).
- Small differences in cross-validation error are within the noise. When the two models are close, the choice matters little for selection, and the simpler model is a reasonable default.

</details>

### The reveal

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Refit the trial of the introduction (spurious-family replicate hook$rep).
seed_h <- BASE_SEED + hook$rep
des_h <- make_design(sa$rep_counts, family_size = sa$family_size, seed = seed_h)
sim_h <- simulate_trial(des_h, h2 = sa$h2, sigma2_family = sa$sigma2_family, seed = seed_h)
dm_h <- design_matrices(des_h)
eff_B <- list(genotype = list(Z = dm_h$Z, G = NULL))
eff_A <- c(eff_B, list(family = list(Z = dm_h$W_family, G = NULL)))
fit_hA <- reml_dense_fit(sim_h$y, dm_h$X, eff_A)
fit_hB <- reml_dense_fit(sim_h$y, dm_h$X, eff_B)
stopifnot(abs(fit_hA$loglik - hook$loglik_A) < 1e-6, abs(fit_hB$loglik - hook$loglik_B) < 1e-6)

# Profile log-likelihood of Analyst A over the family variance ratio.
setup_hA <- .multi_setup(sim_h$y, dm_h$X, eff_A)
gf <- c(0, seq(0.005, 0.45, length.out = 60))
prof_h <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gf, function(g) {
  o <- optimize(function(lg) .multi_eval(c(exp(lg), g), setup_hA)$loglik,
                c(log(1e-3), log(10)), maximum = TRUE, tol = 1e-8)
  e <- .multi_eval(c(exp(o$maximum), g), setup_hA)
  data.frame(s2f = g * e$sigma2_e, loglik = o$objective)
}))
stopifnot(abs(prof_h$loglik[1] - hook$loglik_B) < 1e-4,
          max(prof_h$loglik) <= hook$loglik_A + 1e-6)

# The prose names Analyst B as the more accurate one.
stopifnot(hook$cor_B > hook$cor_A, !hook$degenerate_A, !hook$degenerate_B)
# "A's model also moved part of the genetic variance into the family term."
stopifnot(fit_hA$sigma2[["genotype"]] < fit_hB$sigma2[["genotype"]],
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit_hA$sigma2[["family"]], hook$sigma2_extra_hat, tolerance = 1e-4)))
n_top_A <- round(hook$topk_A * k_top); n_top_B <- round(hook$topk_B * k_top)
```

The trial in the introduction was simulated in the spurious-family world: there are no family effects. It was replicate `r hook$rep` (seed `r format(seed_h, scientific = FALSE)`), chosen as the first trial of that experiment in which Analyst A's likelihood-ratio test was "significant". Analyst B was right. B's predictions had an accuracy of `r fmt(hook$cor_B)`, A's only `r fmt(hook$cor_A)`. Of the true top `r k_top` genotypes, B's list contained `r n_top_B` and A's `r n_top_A`. `r if (hook$cv_mse_A < hook$cv_mse_B) paste0("Cross-validation would not have saved us in this trial: A's cross-validation error was lower (", fmt(hook$cv_mse_A), " against ", fmt(hook$cv_mse_B), "), one of the ", ps$rules[[r_cv]]$k_if_B, " spurious-family trials in which it chose A although B predicted better.") else paste0("Cross-validation would have picked B (cross-validation error ", fmt(hook$cv_mse_B), " against ", fmt(hook$cv_mse_A), " for A).")`

```{r, fig.align="c", fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
ggplot(prof_h, aes(s2f, loglik - max(loglik))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = col_ink, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fit_hA$sigma2[["family"]], colour = col_accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(colour = col_main, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Analyst A's hill for the family variance (the introduction's trial)",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: the truth (no family effect). Orange line: A's estimate, the peak.",
       x = "Family variance", y = "Profile log-likelihood below the peak") +
  my_theme
```

This is Analyst A's hill, now along the family variance (the genotype and residual variances are re-estimated at each point). Its peak sits at a family variance of `r fmt(fit_hA$sigma2[["family"]], 3)`, and the height of that peak above zero family variance, `r fmt(hook$loglik_A - hook$loglik_B, 2)` units, is exactly the gain in log-likelihood that impressed us in the introduction. But the truth is at zero. The extra height came from chance patterns in this one dataset that happened to line up with the family labels. A's model also moved part of the genetic variance into the family term: A estimated the genotype variance at `r fmt(fit_hA$sigma2[["genotype"]], 3)`, B at `r fmt(fit_hB$sigma2[["genotype"]], 3)` (true value `r fmt(sa$h2, 1)`). Having estimated a family effect, A's predictions move each genotype towards the average of its family, and in this world family members are no more alike than any other genotypes, so that move is noise.

That is the whole article in one trial. The peak was higher, but it was in the wrong place, and where the peak sits is what drives the predictions.

### What these simulations do not cover

```{r, echo=FALSE}
n_plots_all <- c(sapply(c("analysts", "baseline", "strong"), function(sc) sum(SETTINGS[[sc]]$rep_counts)),
                 uneven = sum(ru_reps))
stopifnot(all(sapply(c("analysts", "baseline", "strong", "kinship"),
                     function(sc) length(SETTINGS[[sc]]$rep_counts)) == n_geno),
          length(ru_reps) == n_geno)
```

Every result here comes from simulated single trials at one site, with an overall mean as the only fixed effect, independent normal plot errors with one common variance, and the designs described above (`r n_geno` genotypes in `r min(n_plots_all)` to `r max(n_plots_all)` plots). We did not simulate spatial field trends or heterogeneous error variances, multi-environment trials or genotype-by-environment interaction, non-normal traits (counts, scores, binary data), or pedigree relationships: the relationship model uses one simulated genomic $G$ with strong family structure. Where the results may change:

- **Rankings.** They were robust to the variance estimate only when genotypes were unrelated and similarly replicated. Anything that makes genotypes borrow information unevenly (relationships, very uneven replication, unbalanced multi-environment data, spatial models) is likely to make the rankings depend on the variance estimates, as the relationship model and the uneven-replication check did.
- **Larger models.** With several variance components (G&times;E, spatial terms, heterogeneous variances) the hill becomes a surface in several dimensions; boundary fits and convergence problems are more common, and the cost of a spurious term or an unconverged fit can be larger.
- **Interval coverage.** The coverage figures of Myth 3 are for these designs and heritabilities. With more information per trial, intervals from standard errors improve, as in the strong design.

The main points, that log-likelihoods are not comparable across datasets, that a higher log-likelihood does not by itself mean better predictions, and that an unconverged fit reports numbers from the wrong point, rest on how REML works rather than on these particular designs.

### Practical checklist

1. **Do not choose a model because its log-likelihood is higher.** An extra random term that does not exist still raises it in a large share of trials (Myth 1: `r pct(s_sp$p_higher)` with `r n_family` families; in theory about `r pct(p_pos_2)` for a balanced extra term with 2 levels of `r sa$family_size` units each, rising towards 50% as the number of levels grows), and the predictions were then usually worse. For a nested random term, use the boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test (Self and Liang 1987; Stram and Lee 1994), remembering that it is a large-sample approximation (Crainiceanu and Ruppert 2004).
2. **Compare log-likelihoods only between models fitted to the same data, in the same units, with the same fixed effects, by the same program** (Myth 1). For fixed effects use maximum likelihood or the method of Welham and Thompson (1997). Never compare across trials.
3. **Use cross-validation or a proper test to decide whether an extra term is supported, not to predict which model wins on one trial.** Cross-validation adopted the spurious family term far less often than "higher log-likelihood" did, but in our runs it did not beat simply defaulting to the simpler model when the term was spurious. Its advantage is that it also works for models that cannot be compared with a test (cross-validation section). Terms that reflect the randomization (replicates, blocks) stay in the model regardless of any test.
4. **Report heritability, predicted gain and reliability with their uncertainty.** They move directly with the variance estimate, while rankings in a simple genotype model with similar replication barely do (Myth 2). Reliabilities from prediction error variances ignore the uncertainty in the variance components (Kackar and Harville 1984).
5. **With a relationship matrix or very uneven replication, the variance estimate affects rankings too** (Myth 2; VanRaden 2008). In our genomic $G$, with strong family structure, much of the loss was in ranking genotypes from different families against each other. Invest in trials that estimate it well.
6. **Look at the width of the hill.** Use profile-likelihood intervals for variance components and heritability. Intervals from standard errors change with the scale they are built on and do not exist for boundary fits: in our weak design, `r pct(mw$n_boundary / mw$n)` of trials had none, and on the $h^2$ scale `r pct(mw$p_below0)` of the rest reached below zero. Profile intervals covered the true heritability in `r pct(mw$prof_cover)` of all weak trials (Myth 3; Pawitan 2001).
7. **Count and report boundary fits** ($\hat\sigma^2_g$ = 0). They tell you the trial was too weak, not that there is no genetic variance (Myth 3: `r pct(mw$n_boundary / mw$n)` of our weak trials).
8. **Treat "Log-likelihood not converged" as an error for every reported number except, in simple models with similar replication, the rankings.** Run to convergence, check different starting values, and only then compare log-likelihoods or report variance components (Myth 4; Gilmour, Thompson and Cullis 1995).

### Conclusions

A REML log-likelihood answers one question: how well do these variance components explain the data in hand, under this model? It does not answer the question a breeder cares about, which is how well the predictions will rank the genotypes. In our simulations, a higher log-likelihood came with worse predictions when the extra model term was spurious and with better ones when it was real; across replicate trials, the trials with higher log-likelihoods were, if anything, the ones with less accurate predictions; and across datasets the comparison is meaningless.

What matters is where the variance estimates land and how well the data pin them down, though not equally for everything. A spurious extra term whose variance lands above zero changes every prediction, usually for the worse. In a simple genotype model with similar replication across genotypes, rankings are robust to a poor estimate of the genetic variance, but heritability, predicted gain and reliability are not; with relationships among genotypes or very uneven replication, rankings move as well. Weak trials give flat hills, scattered estimates and boundary fits; intervals from their standard errors change with the scale, are missing at the boundary and stray below zero, while profile-likelihood intervals avoid all three. And the solver still has to reach the top of the hill: not because the BLUPs change much, but because every number reported from an unconverged fit, the log-likelihood first of all, is not the number the theory is about.

### Reproducibility

The full code used in this analysis is available on GitHub:

<a href="https://github.com/DidierMurilloF/LikelihoodVsAccuracy" target="_blank">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-181717?style=flat&logo=github&logoColor=white" alt="GitHub">
</a>

<details class="fold">
<summary>Seeds, and what is recomputed when the article is knitted</summary>

All models are fitted with the base-R code in `R/`. `scripts/run_simulations.R` runs every experiment with fixed seeds (replicate *r* uses seed `r format(BASE_SEED, scientific = FALSE)` + *r*) and saves the results in `results/`; `scripts/profile_coverage.R` adds the profile-likelihood intervals of Myth 3 and `scripts/robustness_checks.R` the uneven-replication and within-family checks of Myth 2, with the same seeds. The genomic relationship matrix $G$ of the kinship study is built once with seed `r format(BASE_SEED, scientific = FALSE)`, and the cross-validation folds of replicate *r* use seed `r format(BASE_SEED, scientific = FALSE)` + *r* + `r CV_SEED_OFFSET`, so they do not repeat the random layout of the trial. Knitting the article reads those files for every result over replicates and refits only a few single trials live: the oracle check, the likelihood hills, the AI-REML demonstration and the trial of the reveal.

</details>
